title: Triage first: not every item deserves equal time
description: Sorting a queue into tiers before touching any single chart, so a straightforward encounter and a genuinely ambiguous one don't get the same three minutes by default.

learningObjectives.text: Sort a queue into triage tiers using signals available before opening a chart
Explain why flat, item-by-item review time produces worse aggregate accuracy than triage
Recognise which triage signals are unreliable on their own

contentSections.title: The signals you have before you open a chart

contentSections.body: Monday, 8:40am. Your queue at Fairhaven Medical Group has 214 items in it. You have, realistically, six hours of review time before the day's new charts start arriving faster than you clear them. If you give each item the same ninety seconds, you clear the queue and your accuracy on the hard fifteen percent quietly falls off a cliff — because a routine wellness visit and a four-page oncology consult were never the same amount of work, and treating them as if they were is a decision, even when nobody makes it on purpose.

contentSections.scenario: Before opening a single chart, your queue view shows: confidence score, encounter type, note length, and whether any compliance flag fired (a rule-based check, separate from the AI's own confidence, for things like mismatched patient age and diagnosis, or a procedure code with no matching diagnosis).
contentSections.question: Which of these pre-open signals is the least reliable for deciding how much time an item needs?

options.label: A high confidence score
Note length
A fired compliance flag

feedback.confidence: Right. A high confidence score tells you the note's language closely resembles patterns the pipeline associates with that code — it doesn't tell you the note was read correctly, and it's most dangerous exactly where a wrong code happens to look like a common, well-supported one. High confidence lowers the odds you'll need the full review, it doesn't retire the need for one.
feedback.length: Note length is a genuinely decent proxy — a four-page consult with three comorbidities is reliably going to take longer to verify than a two-paragraph follow-up, almost regardless of what the pipeline proposed. It's not perfect (a long note can be mostly templated boilerplate), but it's honest about what it measures.
feedback.flag: A fired compliance flag is one of your best signals precisely because it's rule-based, not statistical — it caught something structurally inconsistent (age versus diagnosis, procedure versus diagnosis) that needs a human look regardless of how confident the pipeline felt about the code itself.

contentSections.concept: **Triage tiers, in order of what they buy you:** Tier 1 (fast pass) — high confidence, short note, no flags, low-risk encounter type (routine follow-up, wellness visit). Tier 2 (standard review) — the queue's default, most items. Tier 3 (full review) — any fired flag, low confidence regardless of note length, or a note over roughly four pages. The point of naming three tiers instead of reviewing in queue order is that queue order is usually just arrival time, and arrival time has no relationship to review difficulty.

contentSections.body: Fairhaven's queue arrives roughly in the order encounters were closed by clinicians, which clusters by clinic schedule, not by coding difficulty. A batch of six wellness visits closed at 9am sits next to a discharge summary from an ICU stay closed at 9:02am. Reviewing strictly in that order means your attention is allocated by scheduling coincidence. Triage exists to put your best, freshest attention on the items that can actually use it, and your fast pass on the items where a fast pass is genuinely enough — not to skip anything.

One caution: triage tiers are a starting allocation, not a verdict. A Tier 1 item that turns out, thirty seconds in, to have something odd about it — a diagnosis that doesn't fit the visit type, a medication list that doesn't match the stated condition — gets reclassified to Tier 3 on the spot. The tiers manage your time budget across a queue; they never override what you actually see once you're looking at the chart. Triage that can't be overridden by what you find isn't triage, it's just a faster way to miss things.

contentSections.code:
Personal triage rule, six months in:

"If confidence is above 90%, I approve without opening the note.
Only notes below 90% get read."
contentSections.question: What's wrong with this rule?

options.label: 90% is too low a threshold to trust
It skips reading the note entirely for the majority of the queue
It should also check note length before deciding

feedback.threshold: The threshold number isn't really the problem — even a 99% threshold applied this way has the same flaw. Any rule that lets confidence alone decide whether you open the note has already given up the thing a reviewer is for.
feedback.noread: Correct. This isn't triage, it's automated approval with extra steps. Triage changes how much time and scrutiny an item gets — fast pass still means you read the note, just faster, for the specific things that go wrong even in high-confidence cases. A rule that skips reading entirely converts you into the rubber stamp the earlier phase of this track spent five modules arguing against.
feedback.length: Adding a length check would make the rule slightly better calibrated, but it doesn't fix the actual defect — the rule still lets some numeric threshold substitute for looking at the chart, which is the part that can't be delegated to a number.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A fast pass is still a pass — a compressed version of the same judgment, applied to the specific failure modes a confident-but-wrong proposal tends to have (right code, wrong encounter; right diagnosis, missed secondary; a negation the pipeline read past). "Confidence above X means I don't open it" isn't a faster version of review. It's the absence of review with a number attached to make it feel principled.

contentSections.body: Triage sorts the queue by how much scrutiny an item needs before you start — it never decides, on its own, that an item needs none.

contentSections.title: Building a triage pass you can actually run at 8:40am

contentSections.body: Knowing the three tiers exist doesn't tell you how to sort 214 items into them without spending an hour doing it. The sort itself has to be cheap, or triage costs more time than it saves.

contentSections.problem: Sort this six-item slice of Fairhaven's queue into Tier 1 (fast pass), Tier 2 (standard), or Tier 3 (full review), using only what's visible in the queue list — confidence, encounter type, note length, flags.

steps.label: Item A
steps.work: Confidence 96%, annual wellness visit, 1 page, no flags.
steps.why: Every signal points the same direction: routine, short, no red flags, high confidence. Tier 1.

steps.label: Item B
steps.work: Confidence 71%, ED visit, 3 pages, compliance flag fired (procedure with no matching diagnosis).
steps.why: The fired flag alone would push this to Tier 3 even without the low confidence — a structural mismatch needs a human look at what the diagnosis should have been.

steps.label: Item C
steps.work: Confidence 89%, established-patient follow-up, 2 pages, no flags.
steps.why: Nothing alarming, nothing that screams fast-pass either. Default tier: Tier 2.

steps.label: Item D
steps.work: Confidence 99%, inpatient discharge, 5 pages, no flags.
steps.why: High confidence and no flags pull toward Tier 1, but note length and encounter type (inpatient discharges routinely carry multiple comorbidities and a principal-diagnosis decision) pull the other way. Length wins this tie: Tier 2 at minimum, arguably Tier 3 for a first-time reviewer of this encounter type.

steps.label: Item E
steps.work: Confidence 45%, wellness visit, 1 page, no flags.
steps.why: Low confidence on a routine, short note is worth noticing rather than dismissing — it can mean the note was unusually terse, or documented something atypical for a wellness visit. Tier 3, briefly.

steps.label: Item F
steps.work: Confidence 92%, established-patient follow-up, 1 page, compliance flag fired (age/diagnosis mismatch).
steps.why: A fired flag overrides a comfortable confidence score every time — that's what the flag is for. Tier 3.

faded.problem: Sort this new four-item slice the same way.

blanks.prompt: Confidence 94%, telehealth follow-up, 1 page, no flags → tier?
blanks.why: Every signal aligned toward routine and low-risk — the textbook fast-pass profile.

blanks.prompt: Confidence 60%, new-patient consult, 4 pages, no flags → tier?
blanks.why: Low confidence plus a long, unfamiliar-to-the-pipeline first encounter is exactly the profile where a full read earns its time.

blanks.prompt: Confidence 90%, established-patient follow-up, 2 pages, compliance flag fired → tier?
blanks.why: The flag decides this one regardless of the comfortable confidence number next to it.

blanks.prompt: Confidence 82%, wellness visit, 2 pages, no flags → tier?
blanks.why: Nothing alarming and nothing that clearly qualifies for a fast pass either — the honest default.

contentSections.procedure: Sort left to right through the visible queue columns: flag fired means Tier 3, full stop, before you even look at confidence. No flag and confidence below roughly 75% means Tier 3. No flag, confidence above that, and a note under two pages with a low-risk encounter type means Tier 1. Everything else is Tier 2 by default.

contentSections.body: A triage sort that takes longer than the time it saves isn't triage — the rule has to run in the few seconds it takes to glance at a queue row.

title: The two-minute review and what it can honestly cover
description: What a genuinely fast pass can and can't verify, and the specific way a two-minute review turns into rubber-stamping without anyone deciding that on purpose.

learningObjectives.text: State the specific checks a two-minute review can reliably complete
Identify when a fast pass has quietly become no review at all

contentSections.title: What two minutes can actually verify

contentSections.body: A Tier 1 item from the previous lesson — 96% confidence, one-page wellness visit, no flags — genuinely doesn't need the same treatment as a five-page discharge summary. But "doesn't need the same treatment" is not the same claim as "needs no treatment," and the gap between those two claims is where a fast pass quietly stops being a review.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer at Fairhaven times herself on forty consecutive genuine Tier 1 items — actually reading the note, not skimming the code.
contentSections.question: What's the median time she takes per item, in seconds?
contentSections.explanation: A real two-minute review of a short, routine note tends to land closer to a minute and a half than to a flat two minutes — the number in this lesson's title is a ceiling, not a target. What eats the time isn't reading every word; it's three specific checks: does the proposed code match the stated reason for the visit, does anything in the note contradict the code (a symptom described as resolved, coded as active), and is there a second condition mentioned that got no code at all. Those three checks are fast because the note is short and the encounter type is simple — they are not fast because they're being skipped.

contentSections.scenario: A two-minute review of a Tier 1 item.
contentSections.question: Which of these can a genuine two-minute pass reliably cover?

items.label: Proposed code matches the stated reason for the visit
Nothing in the note contradicts the proposed code
An obviously-stated second condition got its own code
The code chosen is the most specific one the documentation actually supports
The code is consistent with the patient's documented history across prior visits

explanation.code_match: Yes — this is a fast, structural check: does the code's description plausibly match the visit's stated purpose. It doesn't require deep clinical judgment, just reading the reason for visit against the code description.
explanation.contradiction: Yes — scanning a one-page note for an obvious internal contradiction ("resolved" language attached to a code marked active, a negation the pipeline seems to have missed) is genuinely quick on a note this short.
explanation.secondary: Yes, if the second condition is stated plainly in a short note — it's a scan for "is there another named condition with no code near it," not a deep specificity judgment.
explanation.specificity: No — confirming a code is the *most specific* one the note supports usually means comparing candidate code descriptions against exact wording, which takes real reading time even on a short note. A fast pass can catch a code that's obviously wrong; it can't reliably catch a code that's technically valid but one level less specific than the documentation supports.
explanation.history: No — checking consistency against prior visits means opening prior visits, which a two-minute pass, by definition, doesn't have time to do. This is exactly the kind of check that belongs in Tier 2 or Tier 3, not Tier 1.

contentSections.synthesis: A genuine fast pass is a fast pass on the *checks it does*, not a shallow pass on all the checks a full review does. It covers three specific, structural things well and explicitly does not attempt the two things — specificity and longitudinal consistency — that need more than a minute and a half.

contentSections.body: Name what a fast pass checks, out loud, before you use it — if you can't name the three things, you're not doing a fast review, you're skipping a slow one.

contentSections.title: Where the two minutes quietly becomes zero minutes

contentSections.body: Nobody at Fairhaven decided one Tuesday to stop reviewing Tier 1 items. It happened the way most of these things happen: a heavy week, a backlog, and a fast pass that got a little faster each day until the note wasn't being opened at all, just the code and the confidence number.

contentSections.scenario: Over three months, a reviewer's average time on Tier 1 items drops from 95 seconds to 20 seconds, with no change in her Tier 1 accuracy on the monthly audit sample — the audit keeps passing.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely explanation?

options.label: She got genuinely faster at the same three checks
The audit sample doesn't contain the errors this shortcut would produce
Tier 1 items have gotten easier over time

feedback.faster: Twenty seconds isn't fast reading — it's not enough time to read a full page and hold three checks in mind against it, no matter how practiced someone is. The audit passing doesn't rule this out on its own, but it's the less likely story once you look at what a passing audit can and can't detect.
feedback.sample: This is the pattern worth being suspicious of. A monthly audit sample is small and, if it's drawn randomly from Tier 1, it's disproportionately likely to be full of the genuinely easy items that would pass even a rubber stamp — a wellness visit really does often just get the obvious code right. A shortcut that fails specifically on the rarer, less-obvious Tier 1 items can survive a small random audit for months while quietly producing errors the audit was never positioned to catch.
feedback.easier: There's no mechanism by which Tier 1 items as a category would get easier over time — the triage sort in the previous lesson already selects for the easy end of the queue. If anything, the encounter mix at Fairhaven doesn't change fast enough to explain a 4x speed change in three months.

contentSections.mechanism: **The audit-blind-spot mechanism:** a small monthly sample checks whether the reviewer's calls were *correct*, not whether the reviewer actually did the checking that correctness depended on. A shortcut that happens to get the right answer on easy cases is statistically indistinguishable, in a small sample, from real review — until the sample happens to include one of the cases the shortcut was never equipped to catch. The audit passing is not evidence the fast pass is real; it's evidence the fast pass hasn't yet been tested against a case that would expose it.

contentSections.body: The honest fix isn't a stricter time minimum — a mandated "you must spend at least ninety seconds" doesn't verify anything either, it just adds a stopwatch to a shortcut. The fix is naming the three checks from the first pod as a checklist you can genuinely feel yourself running, and treating any Tier 1 item where you can't remember running them as a signal to slow down, not a data point to feel good about.
A fast pass that's gotten faster without your checks getting cheaper to run has stopped being review; the giveaway is that you can no longer say what you checked.

title: Batching similar items to keep context
description: Grouping a queue by encounter type or specialty to avoid paying a context-switch cost on every item, and recognising the cases where batching actively works against you.

learningObjectives.text: Group a mixed queue into batches that reduce context-switching cost
Identify when batching by surface similarity groups items that don't actually share context

contentSections.title: What batching actually saves

contentSections.body: Between item 40 and item 41 in her queue, a reviewer goes from a cardiology follow-up to a pediatric well-child visit to an orthopedic post-op check. Each switch costs something real — not just time, but the mental re-loading of a different specialty's normal vocabulary, normal comorbidity patterns, and normal code families. Do that forty times in a morning and the switching cost, paid forty times, is bigger than most people budget for it.

Batching means sorting the queue so items sharing context sit next to each other before you start — same specialty, same encounter type, sometimes the same payer, since payer-specific documentation quirks are their own kind of context. The saving isn't in any one item; it's that item 12 in a cardiology batch benefits from the mental state item 11 already built. You're not relearning what a stress-test note looks like every three minutes.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order you'd actually batch a 60-item mixed queue at the start of a session.
steps: Scan the queue list for encounter type and specialty, without opening any chart
Group items into clusters of roughly similar context (same specialty, or same encounter type)
Run triage tiers within each cluster, not across the whole queue at once
Work each cluster start to finish before moving to the next
contentSections.explanation: Batching happens before triage, not instead of it — you're deciding the order clusters get worked in, then applying the Tier 1/2/3 logic inside each cluster. Doing triage first and batching second would mean re-sorting a triage-ordered list by specialty, which is the same work done twice. And working a cluster to completion before switching matters because a half-finished cluster followed by a different specialty pays the switching cost anyway, with none of the saving banked.

contentSections.body: Batching compounds with triage cleanly: inside a cardiology cluster, you're still doing Tier 1 fast passes on the routine follow-ups and Tier 3 full reviews on the complex admissions — batching changes the *order* items get worked in, triage changes *how much time* each one gets. They're solving different costs (context-switching and misallocated attention) and neither substitutes for the other.
Batching pays back the cost of re-loading context, not the cost of review itself — it works alongside triage, not in place of it.

contentSections.title: When surface similarity isn't real context

contentSections.body: Two items both say "orthopedics" in the encounter-type column. One is a routine six-week post-op check. The other is a workers'-compensation claim for the same joint, with a completely different documentation standard, a different payer relationship, and legal stakes the routine check doesn't have. Batching them together because the label matches can cost more than it saves.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer batches her queue by the "specialty" column shown in the tool, then works straight through a batch of eleven "orthopedics" items without re-checking anything else about them.
contentSections.question: What did the specialty label actually fail to tell her?

options.label: Whether the items share a payer
Whether the items share the same documentation and compliance standard
Whether the items are all in Tier 2

feedback.payer: Payer is one real difference that can hide inside a specialty label, but it's not the deepest one here — two commercial-payer orthopedics visits can still differ enormously in what kind of review they need.
feedback.standard: Right. "Orthopedics" describes the clinical domain, not the encounter's stakes or documentation requirements. A workers'-comp claim inside that specialty carries injury-causation documentation, employer notification timing, and legal exposure that a routine post-op check doesn't — batching by specialty label alone puts a reviewer into the wrong mental mode for that one item, right in the middle of a batch built to avoid exactly that switching cost.
feedback.tier: Tier is assigned separately by the triage pass, and batching by specialty doesn't tell you anything about tier one way or the other — that's not really what the specialty label was ever claiming to do.

contentSections.concept: **Batch on the dimension that actually creates the context-switch cost, not the one that's easiest to sort by.** Specialty is a reasonable default because it usually tracks vocabulary and comorbidity patterns. It stops being a good batching key exactly when an encounter type inside that specialty carries a genuinely different review mode — workers' comp, third-party liability, or a compliance-flagged item. Those get pulled into their own cluster even if the specialty column says they match their neighbors.

contentSections.body: The practical rule: batch by specialty as a first pass, then re-scan each cluster for anything that shares the label but not the actual context — a different payer arrangement, a legal or compliance dimension, an encounter type that's structurally unlike its neighbors. Pull those out into their own small cluster or treat them individually. A batch of ten that's actually nine plus one outlier is still worth batching; pretending the outlier fits just because it fits the label costs more than the switching cost batching was meant to save.

contentSections.scenario: A queue clustered by specialty label.
contentSections.question: Which of these belong in their own cluster rather than their labeled specialty's batch?

items.label: A workers'-compensation orthopedics claim
A routine annual dermatology skin check
A cardiology item with a compliance flag already fired
A second-opinion oncology consult with unusually high legal exposure noted

explanation.wc: Different documentation standard, different payer relationship, different stakes — genuinely different review mode from a routine orthopedics visit despite sharing the specialty label.
explanation.routine_derm: This is exactly the case batching by specialty is built for — nothing about it differs from its labeled neighbors in a way that changes the review mode.
explanation.flagged_cardio: A fired compliance flag already told you, independent of specialty, that this item needs a different kind of attention than its batch-mates — pull it and handle it on its own terms.
explanation.second_opinion: Elevated legal exposure changes what's actually being reviewed for, even though the clinical specialty label is accurate — worth its own attention rather than folding into a routine oncology batch.

contentSections.synthesis: The specialty label is a useful default sort key precisely because it's usually right. The skill isn't distrusting it generally — it's noticing the specific signals (payer type, compliance flag, stated legal exposure) that mean this particular item's label is true but not the whole story.

contentSections.body: A batch is only doing its job if every item in it genuinely shares the review mode the label implies — check for the ones that share the label and nothing else.

title: Knowing when to stop for the day
description: Reading your own fatigue-driven accuracy drop-off honestly, and building a stopping rule that isn't just an arbitrary quota.

learningObjectives.text: Identify personal fatigue signals that predict rising error rate before it shows up in a metric
Distinguish a real stopping rule from an arbitrary quota

contentSections.title: The signals that show up before the errors do

contentSections.body: Item 165 of the day. You catch yourself re-reading the same sentence in the note a third time, still not sure what it says. This is not a new observation, and it is also the single most reliable predictor you'll have all day that the next thirty items are going to be worse than the last thirty — and it arrives well before any error-rate dashboard would tell you the same thing.

contentSections.scenario: A study of reviewer accuracy across an eight-hour shift, tracked by item number rather than clock time.
contentSections.question: Around what item count does per-item error rate typically start climbing, relative to the first fifty items of the day?
contentSections.explanation: The exact number varies a lot by person, by how demanding the queue's mix is that day, and by how someone's sleeping — but the shape is consistent: accuracy holds roughly flat for the first hundred-odd items and then climbs measurably from there, well before an eight-hour day is actually over. The number matters less than the shape: fatigue-driven error is not a cliff at hour eight, it's a slope that starts earlier than a clock-based break schedule usually accounts for.

contentSections.scenario: Personal signals worth tracking across a session.
contentSections.question: Which of these are reasonable fatigue signals — things that show up before an error-rate number would?

items.label: Re-reading the same sentence more than once to parse it
Noticing you stopped checking for secondary conditions on Tier 1 items
It's after 2pm
Feeling irritated at an ambiguous note you'd normally find routine

explanation.reread: A direct, immediate signal — comprehension is measurably costing more effort than it did an hour ago.
explanation.skip_secondary: This is the two-minute-review lesson's warning showing up as a fatigue symptom specifically: a check you'd normally run without thinking about it starts getting skipped, which is exactly the shortcut path from that lesson, just triggered by fatigue instead of backlog pressure.
explanation.time_of_day: Clock time on its own isn't a reliable signal — the same person's fatigue curve shifts day to day with sleep, queue difficulty, and how many breaks they've actually taken. Treating 2pm as a fixed marker ignores all of that.
explanation.irritation: A real, physiologically grounded signal — irritation at ordinary ambiguity is a common early marker of cognitive fatigue, and it shows up before someone would consciously rate themselves as "tired."

contentSections.synthesis: The useful signals are behavioral and specific — what you're doing or feeling differently right now — not a clock. A stopping rule built on clock time misses the days fatigue arrives early and wastes good hours on the days it arrives late.

contentSections.body: Notice the behavior, not the hour — re-reading, skipped checks, and irritation at routine ambiguity all arrive before a dashboard would confirm anything.

contentSections.title: A stopping rule versus a quota

contentSections.body: "I stop at 150 items" sounds like discipline. It's actually a quota wearing a stopping rule's clothes — and the difference matters on the days 150 items arrives at hour four instead of hour seven.

contentSections.scenario: Two reviewers both aim to "know when to stop." One stops whenever she notices two of her fatigue signals in the same hour, whatever the item count. The other stops at a fixed 150 items every day, regardless of how the day felt.
contentSections.question: Which reviewer's rule is more likely to actually prevent the accuracy drop-off from the first pod?

options.label: The fixed 150-item rule — it's consistent and predictable
The signal-based rule — it responds to the actual state driving the errors
Neither — only a supervisor-set limit works

feedback.fixed: Consistency is the appeal, but it's consistency on the wrong variable. A fixed count doesn't know whether today is a good day where 150 items arrives with plenty left in the tank, or a flare day where the same 150 items already cost twice the usual effort by item 90.
feedback.signal: Correct. Fatigue is what actually drives the error-rate slope, and fatigue doesn't track item count on a fixed schedule — it tracks sleep, queue difficulty, and how many genuinely restorative breaks happened. A rule tied to the signals that predict fatigue responds to the thing actually causing the problem, on the day it's actually happening.
feedback.neither: A supervisor-set limit has the same flaw as a self-set fixed count — a number set in advance can't know what today's fatigue curve looks like any better than the reviewer living it. It might set a sane outer bound, but it can't substitute for a signal-based rule inside that bound.

contentSections.mechanism: **Why a quota fails as a stopping rule:** a quota is set in advance, using information available before the day starts (typical daily volume, typical staffing need). Fatigue is a live variable that depends on information only available during the day — how demanding this particular queue mix turned out to be, how much sleep happened last night, whether a Tier 3 item just took forty extra minutes of genuinely hard reading. A rule that can't see that information can't respond to it.

contentSections.body: This isn't an argument against having any outer bound — a workday needs a real end, and a reasonable one exists for planning and staffing reasons. It's an argument for treating the signal-based rule as the one that actually protects accuracy, and the quota as a separate, coarser planning tool that sits around it. The record you keep of your own signals — covered properly in this phase's third module — is what turns "I just felt done" into something you can point to.
A quota tells you when a normal day should end. Only your own signals can tell you when today, specifically, already has.

title: Rebuilding speed after time away
description: A deliberate ramp-up plan for returning to a queue after days away, instead of either matching pre-absence speed on day one or apologising your way through a slow week.

learningObjectives.text: Build a staged ramp-up plan for returning to review work after an absence
Identify what specifically needs re-syncing after time away from a queue

contentSections.title: What actually goes stale

contentSections.body: Six days out with a POTS flare, back at Fairhaven on a Wednesday. The queue looks the same. It isn't — a payer updated a prior-authorization rule on Tuesday, the compliance team added a new flag type on Monday, and your own pattern-recognition for this week's mix of encounter types is six days colder than it was. Nothing about "just pick up where you left off" accounts for any of that.

contentSections.question: Put these ramp-up steps in the order that actually catches what went stale.
steps: Check for anything that changed while you were out — new flag types, payer rule updates, team announcements
Start with a small batch of Tier 1 items to re-sync pattern recognition at low stakes
Move to a normal mixed batch at a deliberately reduced pace for the rest of the first day back
Return to your normal pace and triage rhythm from the second day back
contentSections.explanation: Checking for changes has to come first because everything after it depends on knowing what's different — reviewing Tier 1 items confidently is worthless if a payer rule changed and you don't know it yet. Starting with Tier 1 items specifically (not diving into a Tier 3 backlog) re-syncs judgment at low stakes before anything complex is on the table. And the reduced-pace mixed batch matters because Tier 1-only work doesn't rebuild the harder pattern-recognition a full day actually needs — it's a warm-up, not a substitute for the rest of the day's real mix.

contentSections.body: The specific things that go stale after time away aren't mysterious once you name them: procedural changes (new flags, updated payer rules, a compliance memo that went out while you were gone), and personal recognition speed (the fluency that made a routine wellness visit take ninety seconds instead of three minutes, which erodes measurably after even a week off). A ramp-up plan exists to catch both, deliberately, instead of discovering the procedural gap mid-review or grinding through the recognition gap at full speed and full error rate.
Time away costs you two different things — what changed while you were gone, and how fast you were before. A ramp-up plan checks for the first before it starts costing you on the second.

contentSections.title: A day-one plan you can actually follow

contentSections.body: The alternative to a ramp-up plan isn't usually "nothing" — it's an apology. "Sorry, I'm still getting back up to speed" said to a supervisor after a slow, error-prone morning, instead of a plan that made the slow morning a deliberate, defensible choice instead of a surprise.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer returns after four days out. She spends the first fifteen minutes checking team announcements and a payer bulletin, then works a slow first hour on Tier 1 items only, then returns to normal mixed batches at normal pace for the rest of the day.
contentSections.question: What's the actual purpose of the fifteen minutes at the start?

options.label: It's a courtesy — showing she's being conscientious
It closes the specific gap that would otherwise cause a wrong call she'd have no way of predicting
It's required by Fairhaven's policy

feedback.courtesy: It reads as conscientious, but that's a side effect, not the point — the fifteen minutes is doing real work, not performing diligence.
feedback.gap: Right. A payer rule change or a new compliance flag isn't something a reviewer can reason her way past by being careful — she simply doesn't know it exists until she checks, and "careful" doesn't help with information you don't have. The fifteen minutes converts an invisible gap into a known, closeable one.
feedback.policy: There's no reason this has to be a policy requirement to be worth doing — it's worth doing because of what it actually catches, independent of whether anyone mandated it. Treating it as a compliance checkbox rather than a real step is how it gets skipped on a day someone's in a hurry.

contentSections.concept: **The fifteen-minute check isn't overhead, it's the part of the ramp-up that can't be recovered by working carefully.** Slow, careful review recovers speed and pattern-recognition gaps on its own, over the course of the first day. It does nothing for a procedural change you don't know happened — that gap only closes by actually checking, and checking it first means it can't silently cause a wrong call sometime later in the day.

contentSections.body: This is also the honest answer to the pressure of coming back to a visibly larger queue after time away: a deliberately slower, plan-following first day is not the same thing as being behind. It's the version of "rebuilding speed" that gets you back to full, trustworthy pace by day two instead of a full pace with a hidden, elevated error rate on day one that nobody — including you — can see yet.

A planned slow first day back is a decision you can defend. An unplanned slow first day back is just what happened, and it's indistinguishable from carelessness to anyone looking at the numbers later.

title: Practice — Triage and Time-Budget Seven Simulated Queues
description: Seven drills on the module's skills — sorting queues into tiers, batching, and reading fatigue and re-entry signals. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Apply triage and batching judgment to unfamiliar queue slices at speed
Recognise fatigue and stale-context signals in scenario form

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven drills across triage, batching, stopping points, and re-entry. Nothing new here — this is where sorting a queue stops being something you've read about and starts being something you can do without stopping to think through the rule each time.

Triage, batching, and knowing when to stop are the same skill applied to three different axes of a queue: how much time an item gets, what order items get worked in, and when working stops being trustworthy.

title: Lab — Work a Fifty-Item Queue Against a Time Budget
description: Work a simulated fifty-item queue against a realistic time budget, producing a completed queue with per-item time, decisions, and an accuracy check against the answer key.

learningObjectives.text: Triage and batch a realistic mixed queue under a real time constraint
Produce a defensible per-item time and decision record checkable against a key

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the module's real test: not whether you can explain triage and batching, but whether you can run both, live, against fifty items and a clock, and still land inside an acceptable accuracy band on the ones that mattered most.

contentSections.title: Work a Fifty-Item Queue Against a Time Budget
contentSections.brief: Fairhaven Medical Group's queue has fifty items in it and you have a 90-minute simulated time budget — proportionally scaled down from a real shift so the lab fits in fifty minutes of your actual time. Each item lists confidence, encounter type, note length, and any fired flags. Your job: sort the queue (triage and batching), work it inside the budget, and produce a record of your calls.
contentSections.deliverable: A completed queue log: for each of the fifty items, your assigned tier, your batch grouping, your decision (approve the proposed code, correct it, or escalate), and the time you spent — plus a final accuracy check against the answer key, and one paragraph naming which items you got wrong and why.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Triage and batch the queue
stages.instructions: Before opening any single item in detail, sort all fifty into triage tiers using the visible signals, then group them into context batches. Save your tier/batch assignments — this stage is checkable on its own before you spend any review time.
stages.checkpoint: A tier and batch assignment exists for all fifty items, with no item left unclassified.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Work the batches inside budget
stages.instructions: Work through your batches in order, applying the appropriate depth of review per tier. Log a decision and a time for each item as you go. If you're running over budget partway through, that's real data for stage 4 — don't quietly speed up without noting it.
stages.checkpoint: All fifty items have a logged decision and a logged time, in batch order.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Self-check against the key
stages.instructions: Compare your decisions against the provided answer key. Note which items you got wrong, and for each, whether the error looks like a triage-tier mismatch (you under-scrutinised something that needed more), a batching failure (a surface-similar item that wasn't actually similar), or something else.
stages.checkpoint: A completed accuracy count and an error-type note exists for every item you got wrong.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Write the retrospective paragraph
stages.instructions: In one paragraph, name what you'd change about your triage or batching rule based on what actually went wrong — not a general reflection, a specific rule change you'd make before running this queue again.
stages.checkpoint: The paragraph names a specific, checkable rule change, not a general impression.

rubric.criterion: All fifty items triaged and batched before review began
rubric.meets: No item skipped the sorting stage; tier and batch are recorded for every item.

rubric.criterion: Time budget respected or the overrun is explicitly logged
rubric.meets: The log shows actual time spent per item, including any items where the budget was exceeded, rather than a uniform time that doesn't match the real work.

rubric.criterion: Accuracy on Tier 3 items meets or exceeds accuracy on Tier 1 items
rubric.meets: The whole point of triage is protecting scrutiny on hard items — if Tier 1 accuracy is higher than Tier 3, the time allocation didn't do its job.

rubric.criterion: Errors are classified by type, not just counted
rubric.meets: Each wrong call is labeled as a triage-tier issue, a batching issue, or another named cause — not left as an undifferentiated tally.

rubric.criterion: The retrospective names a specific, testable rule change
rubric.meets: The paragraph proposes something concrete enough that a second attempt at this lab could confirm whether it actually helped.

contentSections.body: The lab's real question isn't your final accuracy number — it's whether your errors cluster where triage should have protected you, or somewhere it never claimed to.

title: Checkpoint — Queue Craft
description: Ten questions pulling from this module. Ungraded, untimed — getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve the module's triage, batching, and pacing distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Retrieval
Checkpoint — Queue Craft
contentSections.framing: Ten questions from this module — this is the first module of the phase, so there's nothing earlier yet to pull from.

questions.prompt: A queue item has a fired compliance flag but a 95% confidence score. What tier?

options.label: Tier 1 — the confidence is high enough to trust
Tier 3 — the flag overrides the confidence score
Tier 2 — split the difference

questions.explanation: A fired compliance flag is a rule-based structural signal, independent of the AI's confidence — it always pushes an item to Tier 3, regardless of how confident the pipeline felt about the code itself.

questions.prompt: What does a genuine two-minute review reliably check, that this module named specifically?

options.label: Code matches visit reason, no contradiction in the note, obvious secondary conditions are coded
Whether the code is the most specific one the documentation supports
Consistency with the patient's history across prior visits

questions.explanation: Specificity checking and longitudinal history checking both take more time than a fast pass has — they belong in Tier 2 or 3, not Tier 1.

questions.prompt: Why is a fixed item-count stopping rule ("I always stop at 150") worse than a signal-based one?

options.label: Fatigue tracks sleep and queue difficulty, not a fixed count, so a fixed number can't see it
It's simply slower to follow
It's unfair to reviewers who work faster

questions.explanation: A quota is set using information available before the day starts; fatigue depends on information only available during the day. A rule that can't see that information can't respond to it.

questions.prompt: Two items both say "orthopedics." One is routine, one is workers' comp. Why doesn't batching them together work?

options.label: They don't share a real documentation and compliance standard, despite sharing a label
They're billed to different departments
Workers' comp items always take longer

questions.explanation: The specialty label describes clinical domain, not stakes or documentation requirements — workers' comp carries injury-causation documentation and legal exposure a routine visit doesn't.

questions.prompt: What's the actual purpose of checking for procedural changes (new flags, payer rule updates) before your first item back after time away?

options.label: It closes a gap that careful review alone can't recover — you can't reason past information you don't have
It's a courtesy to the team
It's just a warm-up exercise for your hands

questions.explanation: Slow, careful work recovers speed and pattern-recognition on its own over the first day back — it does nothing for a procedural change you simply don't know happened yet.

questions.prompt: "If confidence is above 90%, I approve without opening the note" — what's the core flaw?

options.label: It skips reading the note for most of the queue, which isn't a faster review, it's no review
90% is set too low
It doesn't factor in note length

questions.explanation: The threshold number isn't really the issue — any rule that lets a number substitute entirely for opening the note has given up the thing a reviewer is for.

questions.prompt: A reviewer's Tier 1 review time drops from 95 to 20 seconds over three months while her monthly audit keeps passing. What's the likely explanation?

options.label: The small audit sample doesn't happen to contain the kind of error this shortcut would produce
She's genuinely gotten faster at the same checks
Tier 1 items got easier over time

questions.explanation: A passing small sample isn't evidence a shortcut is safe — it's evidence the sample hasn't yet included a case the shortcut was never equipped to catch.

questions.prompt: What does batching save that triage doesn't address?

options.label: The mental cost of re-loading context when specialty or encounter type changes item to item
The total review time budget for the day
Overall accuracy on hard items

questions.explanation: Triage changes how much time an item gets; batching changes the order items are worked in, to avoid paying a context-switch cost repeatedly. They solve different costs and don't substitute for each other.

questions.prompt: Which fatigue signal does this module treat as reliable?

options.label: Re-reading the same sentence more than once to parse it
It's past 2pm
You've reviewed exactly 100 items

questions.explanation: Behavioral signals — re-reading, skipped checks, irritation at routine ambiguity — predict the error-rate slope. Clock time and fixed counts don't, because fatigue's actual timing shifts day to day.

questions.prompt: A Tier 1 item turns out, thirty seconds in, to have something odd about it. What happens to the tier assignment?

options.label: It's reclassified to Tier 3 on the spot — triage is a starting allocation, not a verdict
It stays Tier 1 since the initial sort already decided
It has to be escalated to a supervisor to change tier

questions.explanation: Triage manages time allocation across a queue; it never overrides what you actually find once you're looking at the chart. Triage that can't be overridden by what you find isn't triage.

contentSections.body: None of this sticks by reading it once — that's what this checkpoint, and the ones after it, are for.

title: Accuracy rates in coding: how they're actually calculated
description: What a reported accuracy percentage actually counts — and the specific ways the same underlying performance can produce very different-looking numbers depending on the denominator.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a coding accuracy rate actually counts as numerator and denominator
Identify how denominator choice changes a reported accuracy number without changing performance

contentSections.title: What's actually in the fraction

contentSections.body: Fairhaven's monthly report says you're at 96% accuracy. Riverside Memorial's report, for a coder doing the same volume of the same kind of work, says 91%. Neither number tells you who's better at the job until you know what's sitting in the denominator of each fraction — and the two hospitals don't count the same things.

contentSections.scenario: Two accuracy formulas, both real and both in use somewhere: Formula A counts every code on every claim (a claim with four codes and one wrong code scores 75% on that claim). Formula B counts whole claims (a claim with even one wrong code among its four scores as one incorrect claim, 0% on that claim).
contentSections.question: Which formula produces a lower reported number for the exact same underlying error pattern?

options.label: Formula A (per-code)
Formula B (per-claim)
They always match

feedback.a: Per-code scoring is actually the more forgiving of the two for a coder who gets most codes on a complex claim right — a claim with three correct codes and one wrong one still banks 75% under this formula.
feedback.b: Right. Per-claim scoring is unforgiving of complexity: a four-code claim with a single wrong secondary diagnosis code scores identically to a claim where every code is wrong. This is why a coder working complex, multi-code inpatient claims can show a lower per-claim accuracy than a colleague working simple single-code visits, with no actual difference in per-code skill.
feedback.same: They diverge specifically whenever a claim has more than one code and isn't either fully right or fully wrong — which is most real claims of any complexity.

contentSections.concept: **A coding accuracy rate is always a fraction, and which unit sits in the denominator (individual codes, or whole claims) changes what the number means before any actual performance difference enters the picture.** Neither formula is wrong — they're measuring different things — but comparing a per-code number to a per-claim number, or comparing two people working different case-mix complexity under the same formula, compares apples to oranges while looking like a clean comparison.

contentSections.body: There's a second axis worth naming: what counts as an *error* in the numerator. Some shops count only errors that would change reimbursement (a wrong secondary diagnosis with no payment impact doesn't count against you). Others count every deviation from the correct code set, reimbursement-neutral or not. A shop using the first standard will always report higher accuracy than one using the second, for identical underlying work — which matters enormously if you ever compare a number from one job to a number from another, or if a target gets renegotiated using someone else's benchmark.

None of this means accuracy numbers are meaningless — inside one shop, using one consistent formula, a trend over time is genuinely informative. The caution is specific: don't compare your number to a number from a different formula, a different case mix, or a different reimbursement-impact standard, and don't accept a target that was set using a formula different from the one your own accuracy is measured against without asking which formula is actually in play.

contentSections.code:
Team memo: "Congratulations to Priya for hitting 98% accuracy this quarter,
top of the team — everyone else, aim for her number."

(Priya works single-code annual wellness visits.
Everyone else works multi-code specialist claims.)
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this comparison?

options.label: Priya's number is being celebrated using a different case-mix denominator than everyone else's target
98% isn't actually a good accuracy rate
The memo should have used per-code instead of per-claim scoring

feedback.casemix: Correct. Single-code wellness visits are close to the easiest possible case for per-claim accuracy — nearly every code either matches or doesn't, with little room for a defensible secondary-diagnosis judgment call to go against you. Setting that number as the target for colleagues doing multi-code specialist claims sets a target that's structurally easier for one group than another, using the exact case-mix confound this lesson names.
feedback.notgood: 98% is a fine number in isolation — the problem isn't the number itself, it's using it as an unqualified benchmark across two genuinely different kinds of work.
feedback.formula: Switching formulas wouldn't fix the underlying issue — the case-mix difference between wellness visits and specialist claims would still confound the comparison under either formula, just by a different amount.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A fair accuracy comparison needs matched case mix as much as it needs a matched formula. "Aim for her number" treats a structural difference in task difficulty as if it were a difference in skill — exactly the kind of comparison that turns a measurement tool into a source of unearned pressure.

contentSections.body: Before trusting or comparing any accuracy number, name its denominator and its error-counting standard — the number means nothing on its own.

contentSections.title: What the number is actually for

contentSections.body: If accuracy numbers are this easy to misread, it's worth asking what they're actually good for — and the honest answer is narrower than most dashboards imply.

contentSections.scenario: Uses of a personal accuracy number.
contentSections.question: Which of these are things a well-defined, consistently-measured accuracy rate can honestly support?

items.label: Tracking whether your own accuracy is trending up or down over time
Telling you what kind of errors you're making
Confirming you've cleared the mastery threshold for a module
Ranking you against a colleague working a different case mix

explanation.trend: A consistent formula applied to your own work over time is exactly the comparison that's fair — same denominator logic, same person, just different months.
explanation.errortype: An aggregate rate is a single number — it can tell you *that* something is off, never *what*. That's the specific gap the next lesson exists to close.
explanation.threshold: This is a legitimate, narrow use: the mastery gate just needs to know whether you cleared a bar, and a consistent formula answers that cleanly regardless of what it can't tell you.
explanation.compare_other: This is the exact comparison the first pod warned against — it's only fair if the case mix and formula genuinely match, which is rarely true without checking.

contentSections.synthesis: An accuracy rate is a good trend line and a fine threshold check. It is not a diagnosis, and it is not a fair ranking tool across different people's different work — those need something with more resolution than one aggregate percentage.

contentSections.body: Trust an accuracy number for what it's built to show — your own trend, against your own consistent formula. Ask for something else when you need to know what's actually going wrong.

title: Your error profile is not random
description: Why a coder's errors cluster into a small number of recognisable, personal patterns rather than scattering evenly across the code set — and how to find your own clusters from a list of past corrections.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why coding errors cluster into personal patterns rather than distributing randomly
Identify a recurring error pattern from a list of individual corrections

contentSections.title: Why errors cluster instead of scatter

contentSections.body: A 4% error rate sounds like four claims in every hundred going wrong more or less at random. It almost never works that way. Pull the actual wrong claims and a pattern shows up fast: maybe it's always a secondary diagnosis in diabetic patients with a comorbidity the note mentions in passing. Maybe it's always a specificity miss on musculoskeletal injuries. The 4% has a shape, and the shape is personal.

contentSections.scenario: A coder reviews her last twenty corrected claims. Fourteen of the twenty involve missing a secondary diagnosis code for a condition mentioned only once, briefly, in a much longer note about a different primary problem.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely underlying cause of this cluster?

options.label: Bad luck — fourteen unrelated random errors happened to look similar
A specific reading habit — skimming for the primary problem and under-weighting brief secondary mentions
The pipeline is worse at secondary diagnoses than primary ones

feedback.luck: Fourteen out of twenty sharing the exact same structural shape — brief secondary mention, longer primary discussion — is not what random error looks like. Random error scatters across error types roughly evenly; this doesn't.
feedback.habit: Right. A reading habit — attention naturally gravitating to the note's main narrative and skimming past a single-sentence secondary mention — produces exactly this kind of consistent, reproducible pattern. It's not carelessness in the vague sense; it's a specific, nameable thing the eye does on this specific note shape, every time.
feedback.pipeline: The scenario is about the coder's own corrections to the pipeline's proposals, not about the pipeline's error rate on secondary diagnoses generally — this cluster is diagnostic of the reviewer's reading pattern, not the pipeline's.

contentSections.mechanism: **Why errors cluster:** an error rate isn't the sum of independent coin-flips, it's the output of a small number of recurring cognitive habits — a particular kind of note structure the eye skims past, a particular code family whose specificity rules never quite stuck, a particular clinical scenario that's genuinely ambiguous and gets resolved the same wrong way each time. Naming the habit turns an aggregate percentage into something you can actually work on, because you now know what to watch for instead of just watching everything equally hard.

contentSections.body: This is also why a flat instruction like "be more careful" rarely moves an accuracy number — it asks for more uniform effort across a surface where the errors were never uniformly distributed in the first place. "Slow down specifically on notes with a longer primary narrative and a brief secondary mention" is a instruction that targets the actual cluster; "be more careful" spends the same extra effort everywhere, including on the 86% of claims that were never the problem.
An error rate is an aggregate of a small number of recurring habits, not evenly scattered mistakes — find the habit, not just the number.

contentSections.title: Finding your own cluster from a correction list

contentSections.body: Knowing clusters exist doesn't automatically show you your own. Finding it means actually looking at a list of your corrections side by side, not one at a time as they happen.

contentSections.problem: Here are six of a coder's corrected claims from the past month, briefly summarised. Find the cluster.

steps.label: Claim 1
steps.work: Missed a T2DM-with-neuropathy combination code; coded diabetes and neuropathy separately.
steps.why: A combination-code miss — the pipeline (or the coder) picked two separate codes where ICD-10-CM has a single combined code for the documented relationship.

steps.label: Claim 2
steps.work: Missed that a hypertension diagnosis was documented as related to chronic kidney disease; coded the two as unrelated.
steps.why: Same shape as claim 1: a documented relationship between two conditions that has its own combination code, coded as if unrelated.

steps.label: Claim 3
steps.work: Assigned an unspecified injury code when the note specified laterality (left vs. right).
steps.why: A specificity miss, not a combination-code miss — a different error family.

steps.label: Claim 4
steps.work: Missed a diabetes-with-chronic-kidney-disease combination code, coding both separately again.
steps.why: A third instance of the same combination-code pattern as claims 1 and 2.

steps.label: Claim 5
steps.work: Coded a symptom as a rule-out diagnosis for an inpatient stay when it should have stayed a symptom code per inpatient coding guidelines.
steps.why: A different error family — an inpatient/outpatient guideline distinction, not a combination-code issue.

steps.label: Claim 6
steps.work: Missed a hypertensive heart disease combination code where the note documented both conditions with a stated relationship.
steps.why: A fourth instance of the combination-code pattern — now four of six corrections.

faded.problem: Given this pattern, what's the single most useful thing this coder should do differently starting tomorrow?

blanks.prompt: What specific check should she add to her routine for diabetes, hypertension, and similar chronic-condition claims?
blanks.answer: Check whether the documented relationship between two chronic conditions has its own combination code before coding them separately
blanks.why: Four of six corrections share this exact shape — a documented relationship between two chronic conditions, coded as separate rather than combined. That's specific enough to build a habit around: whenever two chronic conditions appear together with a stated relationship, check the combination-code tables before defaulting to separate codes.

contentSections.procedure: Group corrections by *shape* — what kind of miss happened, not what specific codes were involved — and count. A pattern that shows up in four of six corrections is worth a specific, targeted habit change; a pattern that shows up once is probably closer to noise.

contentSections.body: Grouping corrections by shape, not by specific code, is what turns a scattered-looking list into a pattern you can actually target.

title: Peer review and double-coding
description: How independent double-coding surfaces both real errors and honest disagreement, and running an adjudication conversation that treats disagreement as information rather than a contest to win.

learningObjectives.text: Run a double-coding comparison and classify each mismatch by type
Distinguish a real error from a defensible disagreement in a double-coding mismatch

contentSections.title: What double-coding actually surfaces

contentSections.body: The same chart, coded independently by two people who never saw each other's work, comes back with different codes on one line. Before either person is right or wrong, that mismatch is just information — and the first job is figuring out what kind of information it is.

A double-coding mismatch resolves into one of three categories, and the category matters more than who was right: **a real error** — one coder missed something the note clearly supports, verifiably, once you look; **a defensible disagreement** — the note genuinely supports either reading, and a reasonable coder could land on either code; **ambiguity in the note itself** — the documentation doesn't actually contain enough information to code confidently either way, and the real fix is a documentation query back to the clinician, not a coding decision at all.

contentSections.scenario: A discharge summary documents "acute on chronic systolic heart failure, exacerbation likely related to medication non-adherence." Coder A assigns the combination code for acute-on-chronic systolic heart failure. Coder B assigns only chronic systolic heart failure, missing the acute exacerbation.
contentSections.question: Which category does this mismatch fall into?

options.label: Real error
Defensible disagreement
Documentation ambiguity

feedback.error: Right. "Acute on chronic" is stated plainly in the note, and the combination code exists precisely for this documented relationship. Coder B's omission isn't a defensible reading of ambiguous language — the note says exactly what it says, and one coder simply missed the acute component.
feedback.disagree: There's no real interpretive gap here — the note isn't offering two plausible readings, it's stating the acute-on-chronic relationship directly. This isn't the category where reasonable coders could land in different places.
feedback.ambiguous: The documentation isn't ambiguous — it explicitly names both the acute exacerbation and the chronic condition. Ambiguity would look like a note that never clarifies whether the finding is a new event or a chronic recheck.

contentSections.concept: **The category test:** read the note as if you'd never seen either coder's answer. If the note clearly supports one answer and someone missed it, that's a real error. If the note could genuinely support either reading and a reasonable coder would need to guess between them, that's a defensible disagreement — worth documenting the reasoning for both, not just picking a winner. If the note doesn't contain enough information for either coder to know, coding anything with confidence is the actual mistake, and a query back to the clinician is the right next step.

contentSections.body: It's worth being honest about how often each category shows up: real errors are the minority of mismatches in a mature, well-trained team's double-coding results — most mismatches, once you actually dig in, turn out to be defensible disagreement or documentation ambiguity. Treating every mismatch as "someone made an error" both overstates the error rate and misses the two categories that need a completely different fix (a documented rule for future disagreements, or a clinician query) than more careful coding would provide.

contentSections.code:
Adjudication note: "Coder B was wrong on claim 4471.
Corrective action: retrain on cardiology coding."

(The underlying issue: the note said "possible early-stage
heart failure, awaiting echo confirmation," and both
coders' readings were reasonable given that wording.)
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this adjudication?

options.label: It should have queried the clinician for the echo results before either coder touched the claim
The retraining should cover a broader range of cardiology topics
Coder B should have been given the benefit of the doubt instead

feedback.query: Correct. "Possible... awaiting confirmation" is uncertain, hedged clinical language — exactly the documentation-ambiguity category, not a real error. Neither coder was wrong; the note didn't yet contain a confirmed diagnosis to code. The actual fix is holding the claim (or querying the clinician for the echo result) before finalizing a code either way, not training either coder harder on material the note never gave them enough information to apply.
feedback.broader: More cardiology training doesn't address the actual gap — neither coder lacked cardiology knowledge, the note simply lacked a confirmed diagnosis. Retraining a skill that wasn't the problem doesn't fix the recurring situation.
feedback.benefit: Swapping which coder gets treated as correct doesn't fix the category error — the adjudication is still treating an ambiguity-driven mismatch as if it were a right-answer/wrong-answer situation, just with the labels reversed.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Labeling a documentation-ambiguity mismatch as "Coder B was wrong" manufactures an error rate out of a case where nobody actually erred, and the corrective action (retraining) targets a skill gap that was never the real cause — which means the same situation recurs next time a note says "possible" and "awaiting confirmation," no matter how well-trained either coder becomes.

contentSections.body: Classify a mismatch before assigning blame — real error, defensible disagreement, and documentation ambiguity each need a genuinely different response.

contentSections.title: Running the adjudication conversation itself

contentSections.body: Knowing the three categories doesn't automatically make the actual conversation with the other coder comfortable — especially when the mismatch is on your claim and the honest category turns out to be "real error, and it was mine."

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order an adjudication conversation should actually run.
steps: Both coders independently state their reasoning, before either sees the other's rationale
Compare the two rationales against the note's exact wording
Classify the mismatch: real error, defensible disagreement, or documentation ambiguity
Agree on the resolution and, if it's a recurring shape, document a rule for next time
contentSections.explanation: Stating reasoning independently first matters because it's the only way to know whether a coder actually reasoned their way to an answer or just picked one — if you show your rationale first, the other person's explanation can drift toward agreeing with you instead of reflecting their own independent read. Comparing both rationales against the note's exact wording (not against each other) is what lets you classify honestly instead of just picking whichever explanation sounds more confident. And documenting a rule at the end is what makes a recurring disagreement shape (like the combination-code pattern from the previous lesson) stop costing adjudication time every time it recurs.

contentSections.body: An adjudication conversation is diagnostic, not adversarial — the goal is classifying what actually happened, not deciding who wins.

title: Disagreement that turns out to be ambiguity
description: Recognising the specific note-language patterns that produce genuine ambiguity — not a coding skill gap on either side — and what to actually do about a chart that shouldn't be coded with confidence yet.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise language patterns in clinical notes that produce genuine coding ambiguity
Choose the right next step for a genuinely ambiguous chart instead of forcing a confident code

contentSections.title: The language patterns that create real ambiguity

contentSections.body: "Possible," "suspect," "awaiting," "rule out" — these words don't just make a note sound less certain, they change what can honestly be coded, and missing that is a different failure than missing a fact the note actually states.

contentSections.question: A note reads: "Patient presents with chest pain, rule out MI, EKG and troponin pending." Should this be coded as a confirmed myocardial infarction diagnosis?
contentSections.answer: No — "rule out" language means the diagnosis is being investigated, not confirmed. The correct approach codes the presenting symptom (chest pain) and waits for confirmed results before coding a diagnosis, or per inpatient guidelines, may code the suspected condition differently than a confirmed one depending on setting-specific rules — but never as a flatly confirmed MI.
contentSections.hint: What does "rule out" actually mean clinically — confirmed, or under investigation?

contentSections.scenario: Phrases that appear in clinical notes.
contentSections.question: Which of these phrases signal genuine diagnostic uncertainty that limits what can be confidently coded?

items.label: "Possible early pneumonia"
"Pneumonia, resolved"
"Awaiting biopsy results"
"Confirmed by chest X-ray"
"Suspect early-stage COPD"

explanation.possible: Hedged language — the clinician is stating uncertainty directly, and coding it as confirmed pneumonia would claim more certainty than the note actually contains.
explanation.resolved: "Resolved" is a confident, past-tense clinical statement — there's no ambiguity about whether the condition existed, only about whether it's still active, which is a documented fact, not a hedge.
explanation.awaiting: Explicitly pending confirmation — the note is telling you directly that the diagnostic picture isn't complete yet.
explanation.confirmed: The opposite of a hedge — this is the clearest possible signal that a finding has moved from suspected to established.
explanation.suspect: Another direct hedge word — clinically and linguistically equivalent to "possible" for coding-confidence purposes.

contentSections.synthesis: A small, recognisable vocabulary of hedge words (possible, suspect, rule out, awaiting, likely, probable) reliably signals that a note hasn't yet reached diagnostic confirmation — worth building genuine fluency in spotting these words specifically, since they change what can honestly be coded regardless of how clinically plausible the suspected diagnosis sounds.

contentSections.body: A small vocabulary of hedge words — possible, suspect, rule out, awaiting, likely — reliably marks the line between a confirmed finding and one still under investigation.

contentSections.title: What to actually do with an ambiguous chart

contentSections.body: Recognising ambiguity is only useful if you know what happens next — and "code your best guess anyway" is the wrong answer even when the guess would probably be right.

contentSections.scenario: A coder, under time pressure, codes a "suspected early COPD" note as confirmed COPD because the clinical picture strongly suggests it and she's confident the diagnosis will likely be confirmed later.
contentSections.question: What's the actual risk in coding ahead of confirmation this way, even when the guess is probably right?

options.label: It overstates diagnostic certainty in the permanent record, which can affect future care decisions and billing independent of whether the guess turns out correct
It will definitely be caught in an audit
COPD codes pay less than pneumonia codes

feedback.record: Right. A confirmed diagnosis in the medical record isn't just a billing artifact — it can inform future treatment decisions, risk stratification, and other clinicians' reading of the chart. Coding "suspected" as "confirmed" puts a false certainty into a record that other people will rely on later, independent of whether this particular guess happens to pan out.
feedback.audit: It might or might not get caught — audit likelihood isn't really the point. The problem exists the moment the code is entered, whether or not anyone later reviews this specific claim.
feedback.pay: Reimbursement impact varies case to case and isn't the core issue here — the core issue is putting unconfirmed certainty into a clinical record other people will act on.

contentSections.mechanism: **Why coding ahead of confirmation is a real risk, not just a technicality:** the medical record is read by more than the billing system — other clinicians, future encounters, and risk-adjustment models all treat a coded diagnosis as an established fact. "Probably right" isn't the same claim as "confirmed," and collapsing that distinction for speed exports uncertainty as certainty into a record other people depend on.

contentSections.body: The actual options for a genuinely ambiguous chart, in order of preference: code what the note actually confirms (often just the presenting symptom), hold the claim if your workflow allows pending results, or send a documentation query back to the clinician asking for clarification — a real, standard part of the job, not an admission of failure. "I coded my best guess" should never be a category alongside those three; it's what happens when time pressure crowds out the other options, and it's exactly the shortcut the productivity module later in this phase is built to help you push back on.
An ambiguous chart has three honest responses — code only what's confirmed, hold pending results, or query the clinician. A confident guess is never one of them.

title: Improving one error type at a time
description: Turning a named error cluster into a targeted, checkable improvement — and why trying to fix everything at once produces less measurable change than fixing one thing deliberately.

learningObjectives.text: Design a targeted improvement plan for a single named error pattern
Set a checkable success criterion for whether the improvement actually worked

contentSections.title: Why one error type, not a general resolution

contentSections.body: "I'm going to be more careful next quarter" is the coding equivalent of a New Year's resolution, and it fails for the same reason: it's not attached to anything specific enough to check.

contentSections.scenario: A coder identifies her combination-code cluster from earlier in this module (four of six recent errors) and builds a specific checklist item for it: before coding two chronic conditions on the same claim, check the combination-code tables. She tracks her next thirty combination-code-eligible claims.
contentSections.question: Roughly what reduction in that specific error type would count as a real, checkable improvement — not just normal month-to-month variation?
contentSections.unit: percentage points of error rate on that specific claim type
contentSections.explanation: A targeted checklist item addressing a genuinely identified habit typically produces a large, visible drop on the specific claim type it targets — often cutting that error rate by more than half — precisely because it's aimed at one concrete behavior (checking a specific table before a specific kind of claim) rather than a vague intention. The size of the drop is itself evidence the intervention is hitting a real cause: a small, noisy change would suggest the targeted behavior wasn't actually the driver of the original cluster.

contentSections.body: This is the practical payoff of everything else in this module: a general accuracy number (lesson one) can't tell you what to fix. An error-type cluster (lesson two) can. And a checklist item built around one specific cluster is checkable in a way "be more careful" never is — you can look at the next thirty relevant claims and count whether the specific error recurred, rather than waiting for next quarter's aggregate number and hoping it moved for the reason you think it did.
A targeted fix for one named error type is checkable within weeks. A general resolution to be more careful is checkable never.

contentSections.title: Setting a success criterion before you start

contentSections.body: The improvement plan is only half the job. The other half is deciding, in advance, what would count as it having worked — because deciding that after the fact is how confirmation bias quietly declares victory regardless of what actually happened.

contentSections.intro: Build a real improvement plan for a coder whose cluster is: missing secondary diagnosis codes for conditions mentioned once, briefly, in a longer note about a different primary problem (from lesson two of this module).

fields.prompt: What's the specific, checkable behavior change?
options: Re-read the full note once before finalizing any claim over one page
Be more thorough on secondary diagnoses
Ask a supervisor to double-check every claim
fields.correctValue: Re-read the full note once before finalizing any claim over one page
fields.feedback: The other two options fail the checkability test: "be more thorough" isn't a specific behavior, and asking a supervisor to double-check everything doesn't build the coder's own skill or scale to a normal workload. A deliberate second read on longer notes is specific enough to actually do and specific enough to check whether it happened.

fields.prompt: What's the sample to check the fix against?
options: The next 25 claims over one page
fields.correctValue: The next 25 claims over one page
fields.feedback: The overall accuracy number is too aggregated to isolate this specific error type from everything else affecting the score, and a single claim is too small a sample to distinguish a real change from noise. A defined sample matched to the claim type the error actually occurs in gives a real, checkable read.

fields.prompt: What specific outcome counts as success?
options: Zero missed secondary-diagnosis errors in that sample of 25
A generally good feeling about being more careful
No missed errors, and no other error type increased
fields.correctValue: No missed errors, and no other error type increased
fields.feedback: Zero missed errors alone doesn't rule out a hidden cost — if the extra re-read time led to rushing something else and a different error type crept up, that's not a real improvement, it's a trade. The complete, honest criterion checks both: did the targeted error type actually drop, and did anything else get worse as a side effect.
