contentSections.synthesis: A real improvement plan names the specific behavior, the specific sample it'll be checked against, and a success criterion that accounts for the possibility that the fix helped one thing while quietly costing another — three things a vague resolution to "be more careful" never specifies, which is exactly why it never gets confirmed either way.

contentSections.body: Set the target, the sample, and the success criterion before you start — deciding what counts as success after the fact is how a fix goes unverified either way.

title: Practice — Adjudicate Eight Double-Coding Disagreements
description: Eight drills classifying mismatches and reading accuracy numbers correctly. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Classify double-coding mismatches by type under time pressure
Read accuracy and error-pattern data without the framing errors this module named

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: Eight drills across accuracy formulas, error clustering, and mismatch classification. Do them in one sitting or spread across a couple of days — nothing here expires.

Reading a number correctly, classifying a mismatch correctly, and targeting a fix correctly are the same underlying skill: refusing to let an aggregate stand in for the specific thing that actually happened.

title: Lab — Measure and Analyse Your Own Error Profile
description: Build a real error profile from a simulated set of corrected claims, and produce one targeted improvement plan with its own success criterion.

learningObjectives.text: Classify a set of corrected claims into named error-type clusters
Build a targeted improvement plan with a defined sample and success criterion

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is where lessons two through five stop being separate ideas and become one document: a real error profile, built from data, that names a pattern and a plan checkable enough to actually follow up on.

contentSections.title: Measure and Analyse Your Own Error Profile
contentSections.brief: You're given a simulated set of 22 corrected claims from a Fairhaven coder's past six weeks — each with the original proposed code, the corrected code, and the relevant note excerpt. Build an error profile: classify each correction by type, count the clusters, and produce a targeted improvement plan for the largest one.
contentSections.deliverable: A written error profile: error counts by named type (at least five distinct types named across the set), the two largest clusters identified with concrete examples, and one full improvement plan (target behavior, sample, success criterion) for the single largest cluster.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Classify each correction
stages.instructions: Read all 22 corrected claims and assign each a specific error type (not a vague label — name the actual pattern, the way lesson two's combination-code example did). It's fine to invent a new type name if a correction doesn't fit an existing one.
stages.checkpoint: All 22 corrections have a named error type, and at least five distinct types appear across the set.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Find the clusters
stages.instructions: Count corrections by type. Identify the two largest clusters and pull two concrete example claims for each.
stages.checkpoint: Two named clusters exist, each with counts and two supporting examples.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Distinguish real errors from ambiguity
stages.instructions: Re-read your largest cluster's examples specifically for hedge language (possible, suspect, awaiting, rule out) that might mean some of them were actually documentation ambiguity rather than coding errors. Reclassify any that qualify.
stages.checkpoint: Every claim in the largest cluster has been checked against the ambiguity test from lesson four, with any reclassifications noted.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Build the improvement plan
stages.instructions: For the largest confirmed error cluster (after stage 3's reclassification), write a full improvement plan: the specific target behavior, the sample it'll be checked against, and a success criterion that also checks for side-effect errors elsewhere.
stages.checkpoint: The plan names a specific behavior, a specific sample, and a two-part success criterion.

rubric.criterion: Every correction gets a specific, named error type
rubric.meets: No correction is left as an unclassified miscellaneous item; each has a concrete, repeatable type name.

rubric.criterion: At least five distinct error types are identified across the set
rubric.meets: The classification doesn't collapse everything into one or two overly broad buckets.

rubric.criterion: The largest cluster is checked against the documentation-ambiguity test
rubric.meets: Corrections that turn out to be hedge-language ambiguity, not real errors, are reclassified rather than left inflating the error count.

rubric.criterion: The improvement plan names a specific behavior, not a general intention
rubric.meets: The target reads as something checkable in the next 25 claims, not a resolution to be more careful.

rubric.criterion: The success criterion checks for side effects, not just the targeted error
rubric.meets: The criterion explicitly asks whether any other error type increased, not only whether the targeted one dropped.

contentSections.body: A real error profile survives being handed to someone else — it names specific patterns with specific examples, not a felt sense that some things go wrong more than others.

title: Checkpoint — Measuring Your Own Accuracy
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Queue Craft, two from further back.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and the previous module's core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Retrieval
Checkpoint — Measuring Your Own Accuracy
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four from Queue Craft, two pulling further back.

questions.prompt: Why can two coders doing equally skilled work show different reported accuracy percentages?

options.label: The formula's denominator (per-code vs. per-claim) and case mix both change the number independent of skill
One of them must be less trained
Accuracy numbers are essentially random month to month

questions.explanation: Per-code and per-claim formulas produce different numbers for identical underlying error patterns, and case-mix complexity (single-code visits vs. multi-code claims) further confounds any raw comparison.

questions.prompt: Why do coding errors typically cluster instead of scattering evenly?

options.label: They're the output of a small number of recurring reading or specificity habits
They don't cluster — a 4% error rate is four random errors per hundred
Clustering only happens when the pipeline itself is biased

questions.explanation: A specific reading pattern or a specificity rule that never quite stuck produces the same shape of error repeatedly — naming the habit is what makes an error profile actionable.

questions.prompt: A double-coding mismatch on a note that says "possible early pneumonia" is best classified as:

options.label: Documentation ambiguity — the note itself hasn't reached diagnostic confirmation
A real error by whichever coder didn't code pneumonia
A defensible disagreement between two valid readings

questions.explanation: "Possible" is hedge language signaling the diagnosis isn't confirmed — the right response is coding only what's confirmed or querying the clinician, not treating either coder as wrong.

questions.prompt: What two things does a real improvement plan's success criterion need to check?

options.label: Whether the targeted error dropped, and whether any other error type increased as a side effect
Only whether the targeted error dropped
Whether the coder feels more confident

questions.explanation: Checking only the targeted error can miss a hidden cost — extra time spent on one fix can crowd out attention elsewhere, so a complete criterion checks for that trade explicitly.

questions.prompt: What overrides a comfortable confidence score when assigning a triage tier?

options.label: A fired compliance flag
What time of day it is
Nothing — confidence is always the deciding factor

questions.explanation: A fired compliance flag is a rule-based structural signal, independent of the AI's confidence, and always pushes an item to full review.

questions.prompt: What's the actual flaw in "if confidence is above 90%, I approve without opening the note"?

options.label: It skips reading the note for most of the queue — that's not a faster review, it's no review
90% is too low a cutoff
Nothing — it's an efficient way to triage

questions.explanation: Any rule that lets a number substitute entirely for opening the note has given up the thing a reviewer is for, regardless of the threshold chosen.

questions.prompt: Why does batching by specialty label sometimes fail?

options.label: The label describes clinical domain, not documentation standard or stakes (e.g., workers' comp vs. routine)
It doesn't fail — specialty label is always a safe batching key
Batched items always take longer to review

questions.explanation: A workers'-comp claim and a routine visit can share a specialty label while needing genuinely different review modes.

questions.prompt: What does a confidence score actually measure?

options.label: How closely a note's language resembles patterns the model associates with a code — not a calibrated probability of correctness
A calibrated probability that the code is correct
How fast the pipeline processed the note

questions.explanation: A confidence score is a similarity signal, not a calibrated probability — low confidence from genuine ambiguity and low confidence from an unfamiliar-but-clear rare condition can look identical.

questions.from: How the AI Assigns a Code
questions.prompt: What are the four pipeline stages a note passes through?

options.label: Extract, map, score, route
Read, code, bill, submit
Scan, confirm, file, close

questions.explanation: Extraction identifies clinical concepts, mapping translates them to candidate codes, scoring estimates confidence, and routing decides whether the claim auto-submits or lands in review.

contentSections.body: Retrieval across modules is what keeps the pipeline mechanics from earlier in the track connected to the accuracy-measurement skills you just built — they're the same reviewing judgment, applied at a different zoom level.

title: What productivity targets do to review quality
description: How a volume target, even a reasonably-set one, changes reviewing behavior in specific, predictable ways once someone is behind on it — and why the effect is invisible in the metric that usually gets watched.

learningObjectives.text: Explain the specific mechanism by which a volume target degrades review quality under time pressure
Identify why productivity metrics alone don't reveal this degradation

contentSections.title: The mechanism, not just the outcome

contentSections.body: Fairhaven sets a target of 40 claims a day. It sounds reasonable, and on most days it is. But "reasonable target" and "target that never distorts behavior" are different claims, and the distortion, when it happens, doesn't announce itself — it shows up as a slightly faster Tier 2 review, a secondary-diagnosis check quietly dropped, a hedge word read past. Nobody decides to cut a corner. The target just makes cutting corners the path of least resistance at 3:40pm with eleven items still in the queue.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer is on pace to hit 38 of her 40-claim target with ninety minutes left in the day. At 3:30, she's at 33 with seven items left and forty-five minutes of scheduled time remaining — objectively on track. At 4:15, with fifteen minutes left, she's at 37 with three items remaining.
contentSections.question: What's most likely to change about her review of the last three items, purely from the arithmetic of the situation?

options.label: Nothing — three items in fifteen minutes is still five minutes each, plenty of time
The felt pressure of the countdown itself narrows attention toward finishing, not toward the specific checks each item needs
She'll simply work faster at the exact same quality, since she's had practice all day

feedback.nothing: Five minutes per item is enough time on paper, but the psychological experience of "fifteen minutes, three items, target in sight" is not the same as "five minutes, no clock pressure." The arithmetic being sufficient doesn't mean the felt pressure doesn't change behavior.
feedback.narrow: Right. This is the actual mechanism: a visible countdown against a visible target narrows attention toward the finish line itself rather than toward the specific checks each remaining item needs. It's not that five minutes is objectively too little — it's that the goal quietly shifts from 'review this item correctly' to 'clear this item,' and those aren't the same goal even when they usually produce the same result.
feedback.faster: Working faster at identical quality is the claim worth being skeptical of — it assumes speed and thoroughness trade off at zero cost, which is exactly the assumption the two-minute-review lesson earlier in this phase already challenged directly.

contentSections.mechanism: **Why a target distorts behavior specifically near its own finish line:** a volume target creates a visible, countable goal (items remaining, time remaining) that competes with the actual goal (correct review) for the same attention. Early in a session, with plenty of time left, the two goals don't conflict — there's room for both. Near the end, with the target close and time short, the visible, countable goal (hit 40) becomes more psychologically salient than the goal that has no equally visible counter (catch every error), and attention drifts toward the one you can watch tick upward.

contentSections.body: This is worth being precise about because the honest version of this lesson isn't "targets are bad." A completely unmeasured queue has its own failure modes — nobody notices a backlog quietly growing for weeks. The claim is narrower and more useful: *any* volume target, reasonably set or not, creates this specific end-of-period distortion risk, and the risk is proportional to how close someone is running to the target with how little time left, not to whether the target itself was unreasonable.
The risk a target creates isn't that it's set too high — it's the narrowing of attention toward the countable goal whenever someone is close to it with little time left.

contentSections.title: Why the productivity metric itself won't show you this

contentSections.body: If this distortion is real, the obvious question is why it doesn't show up as a dip in the productivity dashboard. The uncomfortable answer: it shows up as the dashboard looking exactly the same, or better.

contentSections.scenario: Metrics Fairhaven tracks for each reviewer.
contentSections.question: Which of these metrics would plausibly stay flat or improve even while the end-of-day distortion from the first pod was happening?

items.label: Daily claims completed
Percentage of claims completed within SLA
Accuracy rate measured by a small monthly audit sample
A named error-type cluster analysis, if one existed

explanation.volume: Volume improves by definition — the whole distortion is about clearing items faster near a deadline, which the volume metric directly rewards.
explanation.ontime: SLA percentage also improves or stays flat, since the distortion is specifically about finishing on time, not about missing the deadline.
explanation.accuracy: As covered in the previous module, a small monthly sample is disproportionately likely to be full of the easy cases that survive a shortcut — the distortion specifically targets the harder judgment calls (a skipped secondary check, a hedge word read past under time pressure) that a small random sample may simply not happen to include.
explanation.error_type: This is the one thing that would actually reveal it — an error-type analysis targeted at the specific claims completed under end-of-period time pressure, the way the previous module built. None of the standard productivity or aggregate-accuracy metrics do this by default.

contentSections.synthesis: Every metric a typical dashboard shows either directly rewards the behavior that produces the distortion (volume, SLA) or is too coarse to catch it (small-sample accuracy). The distortion is real and invisible to standard reporting at the same time — which is exactly why naming the mechanism, not waiting for a metric to flag it, is the actual skill this lesson is teaching.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to the earlier module's stopping-rule lesson: the honest response to "I'm behind at 4:15 with three items left" isn't to speed up the last three — it's the same signal-based judgment from that lesson, applied to a different trigger. A rushed final stretch is worth naming out loud, even just to yourself, as exactly what it is.
The metrics that get watched by default reward or ignore this exact distortion — the safeguard has to be your own naming of the mechanism, not a dashboard flagging it for you.

title: Saying a target is unsafe, with evidence
description: Building a specific, evidence-backed case that a target is producing unsafe review quality — instead of either silently absorbing it or complaining without anything checkable behind the complaint.

learningObjectives.text: Build an evidence-based case that a productivity target is degrading review quality
Distinguish a checkable claim about a target from a general complaint

contentSections.title: What makes a claim about a target checkable

contentSections.body: "The target is too aggressive" gets nowhere in a real conversation with a supervisor, not because it's wrong, but because it isn't checkable — there's nothing in it a supervisor can verify, dispute, or act on beyond a shrug.

A checkable claim about a target names three things: the specific behavior the target is producing (not "I feel rushed," but "I skip the secondary-diagnosis check on the last four to six items of the day"), the evidence that this is actually happening (a self-tracked log across real days, not a single bad afternoon), and a proposed change that's specific enough to evaluate ("reduce to 34 with a documented queue-difficulty adjustment" beats "lower the target"). A supervisor can engage with all three. A supervisor can only nod politely at a feeling.

contentSections.code:
Message to supervisor:

"Hey, the 40-item target is really stressful and I don't
think it's realistic. Can we talk about lowering it?"
contentSections.question: What's the biggest structural problem with this message, independent of whether the underlying concern is valid?

options.label: It names a feeling (stressful) instead of a specific behavior the target produces
It should have been sent as a formal complaint instead of a casual message
40 items isn't actually an unreasonable target

feedback.feeling: Correct. "Stressful" and "not realistic" are both real, but neither is checkable — a supervisor has no way to verify or act on a feeling. Compare this to "I've tracked my last two weeks and I skip the secondary-diagnosis check on 3 of the last 5 items most days once I'm behind after 3pm" — that's a claim with something to actually respond to.
feedback.formal: The channel isn't really the issue — a casual message could carry a specific, evidence-backed claim just as well as a formal one. The problem is what's inside the message, not its formality.
feedback.unreasonable: Whether 40 is reasonable in the abstract isn't actually knowable from outside — that's exactly why the lesson's approach is to gather evidence about what the target actually does to review behavior, rather than debate the number itself in the abstract.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A message built around a feeling invites a feeling back — reassurance, a "we hear you," maybe a small adjustment nobody can point to a reason for. A message built around a specific, tracked behavior and its evidence invites an actual decision, because it gives the other person something concrete to evaluate against.

contentSections.body: A checkable claim names the specific behavior, the tracked evidence, and a specific proposed change — a feeling, however real, gives a supervisor nothing to act on.

contentSections.title: Gathering the evidence without waiting for a crisis

contentSections.body: The evidence a checkable claim needs doesn't appear after one bad week — it has to be gathered deliberately, in a form that would survive being shown to someone else.

contentSections.problem: Build a two-week evidence log tracking whether the 40-item target correlates with a specific quality cost.

steps.label: What to log
steps.work: Each day: total items completed, time the target was hit or missed, and — for the last four items of each day specifically — whether the full secondary-diagnosis and specificity checks from earlier modules were actually run.
steps.why: Logging the last four items specifically, not all forty, targets exactly the window where the previous lesson's mechanism predicts distortion — a flat daily log wouldn't isolate the effect.

steps.label: What the two weeks show
steps.work: On 7 of 10 days, at least one of the last four items skipped the specificity check that was run consistently on the first thirty-six items that day.
steps.why: This is the specific, checkable pattern — not a vague sense of being rushed, but a documented, repeatable gap between early-day and late-day thoroughness.

steps.label: What this evidence supports
steps.work: A claim that the current target's last-hour pressure correlates with a specific, named quality gap, on a majority of tracked days.
steps.why: This is now a claim a supervisor can respond to concretely: adjust the target, adjust the daily schedule, or investigate why the last four items specifically are the pressure point.

faded.problem: You suspect the target also affects batching discipline (from the first module) late in the day — batches get abandoned mid-cluster to grab whatever's fastest. Design the tracking for this second hypothesis.

blanks.prompt: What specific behavior would you log each day to test this?
blanks.answer: Whether a batch cluster was worked to completion or abandoned partway through, specifically in the last hour of the day
accept: whether batches finished or were abandoned late in day
blanks.why: This targets the exact mechanism suspected — batching discipline breaking down specifically under end-of-day pressure — rather than a general note about feeling rushed.

contentSections.procedure: A useful evidence log targets the specific window where the suspected mechanism operates (the last few items, the last hour), tracks a specific behavior (not a feeling), and runs long enough (two weeks, not two days) to distinguish a real pattern from one unusually bad afternoon.

contentSections.body: Evidence worth bringing to a supervisor is gathered deliberately, targeted at the specific window a mechanism predicts, and collected over enough days to rule out a single bad afternoon.

title: Tracking your own throughput honestly
description: Keeping a personal throughput record that resists the specific temptation to round favorably, and why an honest record protects you better than an optimistic one.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the common ways a self-tracked throughput record gets quietly inflated
Build a throughput tracking habit that resists those specific distortions

contentSections.title: How a self-tracked number drifts

contentSections.body: Nobody sets out to inflate their own throughput record. It drifts — a borderline item counted as "basically done" at day's end, a break not logged because it was short, a Tier 3 item that took twenty-five minutes remembered as fifteen by the time it gets written down an hour later.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer logs her time per item at the end of each day, from memory, rather than in real time as she works. Over a month, her logged average time-per-item is 4.1 minutes; a system timestamp audit of the same period shows an actual average of 5.3 minutes.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely source of this specific gap?

options.label: She's lying deliberately to look more productive
End-of-day recall systematically underestimates the harder items, which take longer and are harder to remember accurately
The system timestamps are simply wrong

feedback.lying: Deliberate falsification is possible but it's the less likely and less useful explanation for a gap this size — it also isn't the failure mode worth building a habit around, since someone deliberately lying isn't going to be fixed by a better tracking method.
feedback.recall: Right. Memory for time-on-task is unreliable in a specific, predictable direction: routine items blur together and feel faster in retrospect, while the genuinely hard items get remembered but their duration gets compressed too, because an hour later, twenty-five focused minutes doesn't feel as long as it was. This isn't dishonesty — it's how memory for effortful time actually works, which is exactly why end-of-day recall is the wrong method regardless of anyone's intentions.
feedback.system: System timestamps recording actual start and stop times are the more reliable source here by construction — they're not vulnerable to the memory distortion the other two options are about.

contentSections.concept: **Honest tracking isn't a character trait, it's a method choice.** The gap between logged and actual time in this scenario isn't explained by dishonesty — it's explained by using a tracking method (end-of-day recall) that's structurally biased toward underestimating exactly the items that took real judgment. Real-time logging, or a system-generated timestamp where available, removes the distortion at the method level instead of requiring anyone to somehow remember more accurately.

contentSections.body: The stakes of this aren't abstract. An inflated self-tracked average makes a target look more achievable than it actually is, which feeds directly back into the previous lesson's evidence-gathering — a supervisor evaluating whether a target is unsafe, working from a throughput log that's already quietly optimistic, will reasonably conclude the target is fine. The record has to be honest before it can be useful for anything downstream, including advocating for yourself.
A throughput record that drifts favorable isn't usually dishonesty — it's end-of-day recall doing what memory for effortful time always does. Fix the method, not the person.

contentSections.title: A tracking habit that resists the drift

contentSections.body: Knowing recall drifts doesn't automatically produce a better habit — that takes a specific, low-friction method that survives an actual busy day, not just a demo day.

contentSections.question: Put these throughput-tracking practices in order from most reliable to least reliable.
steps: A system-generated timestamp for each item's start and stop, if the tool provides one
A logged note at the moment you move to the next item (real-time, one line)
A tally at natural breakpoints — end of each batch cluster, not end of day
End-of-day recall from memory
contentSections.explanation: System timestamps are the most reliable because they're not vulnerable to memory at all — the tool records the moment, not a person's later reconstruction of it. Real-time logging at the point of moving on is close behind, since the memory gap is seconds, not hours. Batch-cluster breakpoints are a reasonable middle ground when real-time logging is too disruptive — the gap is still small enough (maybe twenty minutes) to be fairly reliable. End-of-day recall is last because it has the largest gap between the event and the recording of it, which is exactly where the drift in the first pod comes from.

contentSections.body: The practical version of this doesn't have to be elaborate — a one-line note at each item transition ("item 14 done, 6 min, secondary check run") takes seconds and removes almost all of the recall distortion. The habit matters more than the tool: whatever removes the hour-plus gap between doing the work and recording it is doing the actual job.
The closer a tracking method sits to the actual moment of work, the less it can drift — pick the closest method your workflow actually allows, not the most convenient one at day's end.

title: Negotiating accommodation without disclosing more than you want
description: Asking for a workable accommodation — a flexed schedule, a different daily target, a modified queue mix — using functional language that describes what's needed rather than a full medical disclosure nobody's owed.

learningObjectives.text: Frame an accommodation request in functional, not diagnostic, terms
Distinguish what an employer needs to know from what a coder might feel pressured to share

contentSections.title: Functional language versus diagnostic language

contentSections.body: "I have POTS and some days I can barely sit upright" and "I need the option to split my shift into two four-hour blocks on days I flag in advance" are asking for the same accommodation. Only one of them requires anyone to know anything about a diagnosis.

contentSections.scenario: A coder drafting an accommodation request for a flexible daily target on variable-capacity days.
contentSections.question: Which version gives the employer what they actually need to evaluate and grant the request, without more disclosure than necessary?

options.label: "I have a chronic illness that causes unpredictable fatigue and I need flexibility"
"On days I flag by 9am, I need a reduced target of 25 items with the difference made up over the following two days"
"Please just trust me that I need this, I'd rather not go into detail"

feedback.diagnosis: This discloses a specific condition without actually specifying what's needed operationally — a supervisor still has to guess at what "flexibility" means in practice, and the diagnosis itself adds nothing to that guess. The disclosure is doing work the functional description could do without it.
feedback.functional: Right. This names exactly what changes (a reduced target, on flagged days, made up over a defined window) without requiring any diagnosis, symptom description, or medical detail. It's also the version that's actually easiest for a supervisor to evaluate and approve, because it's concrete and bounded.
feedback.vague: This asks for trust without giving the supervisor anything concrete to evaluate — it's likely to produce more probing questions, not fewer, because there's nothing specific on the table to simply approve.

contentSections.concept: **A functional accommodation request describes the operational need and its shape — what changes, under what trigger, for how long — without describing the underlying medical cause.** Most workplaces, including under formal accommodation processes, are entitled to know enough to evaluate whether a request is reasonable and how to implement it; they are not entitled to a diagnosis, and a specific, bounded functional request usually gets approved faster than a vague one precisely because there's less to interrogate.

contentSections.body: This connects directly to the honest tracking habit from the previous lesson: a functional request is much easier to make credibly if there's already a real throughput record behind it — "I need this because my flagged-day output data shows X" is a stronger request than "I need this because I feel like I need it," for exactly the checkability reason the second lesson of this module named. The record built for one purpose (arguing a target is unsafe) turns out to support a completely different conversation too.
Name what changes, what triggers it, and for how long — that's what an accommodation request needs. A diagnosis isn't on that list.

contentSections.title: Where the pressure to over-disclose actually comes from

contentSections.body: The pressure to say more than needed rarely comes from a form. It comes from a supervisor's raised eyebrow, an uncomfortable silence after a request, or the sense that a bare functional ask sounds like you're hiding something.

contentSections.code:
Supervisor: "I need to understand what's actually going on before I can approve this."

Coder's internal reaction: "I guess I have to explain the whole diagnosis
or this won't get approved."
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in the coder's internal reaction?

options.label: "What's actually going on" can be answered with more functional detail, not medical detail
The supervisor is right — a diagnosis really is required here
The request should be withdrawn if the supervisor pushes back at all

feedback.functional: Correct. "What's actually going on" is an ambiguous prompt that can be answered honestly and completely with more functional specificity — how often flagged days happen, roughly, what the reduced target looks like in practice, how the made-up work gets scheduled — without crossing into diagnosis or symptom description. The supervisor's question doesn't specify medical detail; the coder's internal translation of it does.
feedback.required: In most accommodation frameworks, a functional description of the limitation and need is what's actually required to evaluate a reasonable accommodation — a diagnosis is a separate, more invasive disclosure that isn't automatically owed just because a request needs explaining.
feedback.withdraw: Pushback on an unclear request is normal and doesn't mean the request itself was wrong to make — the right response is more functional clarity, not retreat.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The instinct to escalate to diagnostic disclosure under any pushback treats "explain more" and "explain medically" as the same instruction. They aren't. More functional detail — concrete, bounded, operational — usually answers the actual underlying question (can this be implemented, is it reasonable) better than a diagnosis would anyway, since a diagnosis alone doesn't tell a supervisor what to actually do differently.

contentSections.body: When a request meets pushback, add functional specificity, not medical disclosure — "explain more" and "explain the diagnosis" are not the same request, even when they're said to sound like they are.

title: The record you keep for yourself
description: Building a personal record — separate from anything a supervisor sees — that documents your own patterns, decisions, and the reasoning behind them, for your own protection and your own use.

learningObjectives.text: Identify what belongs in a personal working record versus what goes to a supervisor
Build a sustainable personal record-keeping habit

contentSections.title: What a personal record is actually for

contentSections.body: Six months from now, a claim gets challenged. Or a target gets renegotiated. Or a pattern you half-noticed turns out to matter. The record that answers any of those questions has to already exist — it can't be reconstructed from memory on the day it's needed.

contentSections.scenario: Candidate contents for a personal working record.
contentSections.question: Which of these belong in a coder's own kept record, distinct from anything sent to a supervisor?

items.label: The reasoning behind a genuinely close call, at the time you made it
Real-time throughput and time-per-item data, from lesson three
Your own named error clusters from the previous module
Detailed medical symptom logs unrelated to work decisions
Documentation gaps you flagged but that weren't resolved before the claim was finalized

explanation.reasoning: Recording your own reasoning on a close call at the time you made it is exactly the kind of thing memory distorts (per lesson three) and that matters enormously if that specific claim is challenged later — "here's what I actually thought, in the moment" beats a reconstructed justification every time.
explanation.throughput: This is the same honest tracking from lesson three, and it's yours to keep regardless of whether a supervisor ever asks for it — it's the raw material for any future evidence-based conversation.
explanation.error_clusters: Your own error pattern analysis from the previous module belongs here as a living document, updated as new clusters get identified and old ones get resolved.
explanation.diagnosis: This lesson's record is a working record for work decisions — general medical symptom tracking, disconnected from any specific work decision it might inform, belongs somewhere else (a personal health record) and mixing it in here doesn't serve the record's actual purpose.
explanation.flagged_gaps: A documentation gap you noticed and flagged, even if it wasn't resolved before you had to finalize the claim, is exactly the kind of thing that protects you later — it shows the gap wasn't invisible to you, it was raised and the resolution simply didn't happen in time.

contentSections.synthesis: The unifying test: does this entry document a work decision, its reasoning, or evidence relevant to a future work conversation? If yes, it belongs in the working record. General health information that isn't tied to a specific work decision belongs elsewhere — the working record stays narrowly useful by staying narrowly scoped.

contentSections.body: A personal working record holds reasoning, throughput, error patterns, and flagged gaps — the things memory distorts and a future conversation might need. It isn't a health diary.

contentSections.title: Making the record sustainable

contentSections.body: A record that takes ten minutes a day gets abandoned by week three. The habit that survives is the one cheap enough to do on the worst day, not just the good ones.

contentSections.scenario: A coder builds a lightweight record: one-line transition notes plus occasional close-call notes plus a weekly five-minute skim.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many extra minutes per week does this realistically add to her workload?
contentSections.explanation: The transition notes cost almost nothing extra since they're the same habit as the throughput tracking from lesson three, already built. The occasional close-call notes and the weekly skim are the real addition, and they land around half an hour a week for most people — small enough to survive a bad week, unlike a system that needs daily deliberate effort to maintain. A record system that costs more than this is a record system that gets abandoned exactly when a flare or a busy stretch makes it most needed.

contentSections.body: The realistic version of this record is small and consistent: a one-line note at each item transition (already covered in lesson three's throughput habit), a slightly longer note only on the genuinely close calls (maybe two or three a week, not every item), and a five-minute end-of-week pass to skim for anything worth pulling into the error-cluster or evidence-log documents from earlier in this module. That's the whole system — not a separate elaborate journal, but a habit layered onto tracking that's already happening for other reasons.
The record that survives a bad week is the one built cheap from the start — layered onto habits already in place, not a separate system that needs its own daily discipline.

title: Practice — Draft Seven Responses to Unsafe Target Pressure
description: Seven drills on building checkable claims, honest tracking, and functional accommodation language. No new concepts.

learningObjectives.text: Draft checkable claims and functional requests under realistic constraints
Identify tracking and disclosure pitfalls in scenario form

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: Seven drills across evidence-building, honest tracking, and functional accommodation language. Nothing new — this is where naming the mechanism turns into being able to write the actual sentence.
Checkable evidence, honest tracking, and functional language are the same underlying discipline — say the specific, bounded thing, not the feeling.

title: Lab — Build an Evidence Pack for a Target Renegotiation
description: Build a real evidence pack — throughput data, accuracy data, and a specific proposed target — for renegotiating an unsafe productivity target.

learningObjectives.text: Assemble throughput and accuracy evidence into a checkable case for target renegotiation
Propose a specific, defensible replacement target

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: This is the module's real test: not explaining why targets distort behavior, but building the actual document that would get a specific target changed.

contentSections.title: Build an Evidence Pack for a Target Renegotiation
contentSections.brief: You're given two weeks of simulated data for a Fairhaven coder working a 40-item daily target: daily completion counts, timestamps for each item, and audit-flagged errors by item position in the day. Build an evidence pack that makes a checkable case for a specific target change.
contentSections.deliverable: A written evidence pack: a throughput summary (using honest, real-time-sourced data, not recall), an analysis of where in the day errors cluster, and one specific, bounded proposed target change with the reasoning that connects the data to the proposal.

stages.title: Stage 1 — Build the honest throughput summary
stages.instructions: From the provided timestamp data, calculate real average time-per-item and completion rate. Flag any discrepancy between what a recall-based log might have shown and what the timestamps actually show.
stages.checkpoint: A throughput summary exists, sourced from timestamps, with any recall-vs-actual discrepancy noted.

stages.title: Stage 2 — Find where errors cluster by day position
stages.instructions: Using the audit-flagged errors, determine whether errors concentrate in a particular window of the day (e.g., the last several items) rather than distributing evenly.
stages.checkpoint: A specific day-position pattern is identified and quantified, or explicitly ruled out if the data doesn't show one.

stages.title: Stage 3 — Propose a specific target change
stages.instructions: Using stages 1 and 2, propose one specific, bounded change (a new number, a schedule adjustment, or both) with the reasoning connecting it directly to the data.
stages.checkpoint: The proposal names a specific number or schedule change, not a vague direction, with reasoning that cites the actual data.

stages.title: Stage 4 — Write the pack's summary page
stages.instructions: Write a one-page summary suitable for handing directly to a supervisor: the finding, the evidence, the proposal.
stages.checkpoint: The summary page could be read cold by someone who hasn't seen the raw data and still follow the case.

rubric.criterion: Throughput data is sourced from timestamps, not simulated recall
rubric.meets: The summary explicitly distinguishes what real-time data shows versus what an end-of-day estimate might have shown.

rubric.criterion: The error-clustering analysis is quantified, not impressionistic
rubric.meets: A specific window (e.g., 'items 35-40') and a specific rate difference are named, not a general sense that errors happen 'more at the end.'

rubric.criterion: The proposed change is specific and bounded
rubric.meets: A concrete number or schedule change is named — not 'lower the target' without a figure.

rubric.criterion: The reasoning connects data to proposal explicitly
rubric.meets: Each part of the proposal traces back to a specific piece of evidence in stages 1 or 2, not an unsupported assertion.

rubric.criterion: The summary page stands alone
rubric.meets: A reader unfamiliar with the raw data can follow the finding, evidence, and proposal from the summary page alone.

contentSections.body: An evidence pack succeeds when every claim in it traces to a specific number in the data — that traceability is what separates it from the feeling-based complaint the module opened by rejecting.

title: Checkpoint — Productivity, Targets and Honesty
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from Measuring Your Own Accuracy, two from further back.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's and recent modules' core distinctions without looking them up

contentSections.title: Retrieval
Checkpoint — Productivity, Targets and Honesty
contentSections.framing: Four questions from this module, four from Measuring Your Own Accuracy, two pulling further back.

questions.prompt: Why does review quality tend to degrade specifically near the end of a target period, not evenly across it?

options.label: The visible, countable goal (items remaining) becomes more psychologically salient than the uncountable one (catching every error) as time runs short
Reviewers are always more tired at the end of a shift than the beginning
It doesn't degrade unevenly — the effect is spread evenly across the whole day

questions.explanation: A visible countdown against a visible target narrows attention toward finishing rather than toward the specific checks each item needs — this is a distinct mechanism from general fatigue.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't a standard productivity dashboard reveal the end-of-period quality distortion?

options.label: Volume and on-time metrics directly reward the exact behavior that produces the distortion
Dashboards are generally unreliable and shouldn't be trusted for anything
It does reveal it — that's exactly what a dip in volume would show

questions.explanation: Volume and SLA metrics improve or stay flat precisely because the distortion is about finishing on time, not missing deadlines — and small-sample accuracy audits are too coarse to catch it reliably.

questions.prompt: What three things does a checkable claim that a target is unsafe need to name?

options.label: The specific behavior produced, the tracked evidence, and a specific proposed change
How stressful the target feels and why it should be lowered
Just the proposed new number

questions.explanation: A feeling gives a supervisor nothing to verify or act on; a specific behavior, tracked evidence, and a bounded proposal give them something they can actually evaluate.

questions.prompt: What makes a functional accommodation request different from a diagnostic disclosure?

options.label: It names what changes, what triggers it, and for how long, without describing the underlying medical cause
They're the same thing, just phrased differently
A functional request is always less likely to be approved

questions.explanation: A functional request describes the operational need and its bounds; most accommodation processes need exactly that, not a diagnosis, and bounded requests are often easier to evaluate and approve.

questions.prompt: Why can two coders doing equally skilled work show different accuracy percentages?

options.label: Formula (per-code vs. per-claim) and case mix both change the number independent of skill
One of them is definitely less skilled
The numbers are essentially random

questions.explanation: Denominator choice and case-mix complexity confound raw accuracy comparisons before any real skill difference is considered.

questions.prompt: A double-coding mismatch on a note reading "suspect early COPD" should be classified as:

options.label: Documentation ambiguity
A real error by whoever didn't code COPD
A defensible disagreement between two valid readings

questions.explanation: "Suspect" is hedge language signaling the diagnosis isn't confirmed — coding anything with confidence, or blaming either coder, misreads the actual situation.

questions.prompt: Why do coding errors typically cluster rather than scatter evenly?

options.label: They're the output of a small number of recurring reading or specificity habits
They're genuinely random and don't cluster
Clustering only happens because of pipeline bugs

questions.explanation: A specific reading pattern or specificity gap produces the same error shape repeatedly, which is what makes a targeted fix possible.

questions.prompt: A complete improvement-plan success criterion checks for what two things?

options.label: Whether the targeted error dropped, and whether any other error type increased as a side effect
Only whether the targeted error dropped
Whether review got faster overall

questions.explanation: Checking only the targeted metric can miss a hidden cost from the extra attention or time the fix required.

questions.prompt: What's the actual purpose of checking for procedural changes before your first item back after time away?

options.label: It closes a gap careful review alone can't recover — you can't reason past information you don't have
It's a courtesy to the team
It's required by policy and otherwise has no real purpose

questions.explanation: Slow, careful work recovers speed and recognition gaps on its own — it does nothing for a procedural change you simply don't know happened.

questions.from: How the AI Assigns a Code
questions.prompt: What do the four pipeline stages, in order, actually do?

options.label: Extract concepts, map to candidate codes, score confidence, route to auto-submit or review
Read, code, bill, submit
Scan, confirm, file, close

questions.explanation: Each stage depends on the one before it, which is why diagnosing which stage produced a given error changes both how much to trust the rest of the proposal and what to flag if the pattern repeats.

contentSections.body: Targets, tracking, and disclosure all come back to the same discipline this checkpoint is testing: naming the specific mechanism instead of the general feeling.

title: Encoders, groupers and what they decide for you
description: What an encoder and a DRG grouper each actually do beneath the interface — and why trusting a grouper's output without understanding its inputs is a different failure than trusting the AI pipeline's proposed code.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish what an encoder does from what a DRG grouper does
Identify which grouper inputs a reviewer is responsible for verifying before trusting its output

contentSections.title: Two different tools, two different jobs

contentSections.body: "The encoder" and "the grouper" get used interchangeably in casual conversation at Fairhaven, and that looseness costs people real time the first month on the job — they're different tools, they take different inputs, and confusing what each one is actually deciding for you is how a wrong grouper output gets blamed on the encoder, or vice versa, and nobody fixes the actual problem.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer enters a set of ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS codes for an inpatient stay. One tool checks each code against its own coding conventions and flags an invalid code combination. A second, separate tool takes the final validated code set plus a few other inputs (discharge status, principal diagnosis, presence of major complications) and outputs a DRG (Diagnosis-Related Group) with an associated relative weight.
contentSections.question: Which tool is the encoder, and which is the grouper?

options.label: The first tool (code validation) is the encoder; the second (DRG assignment) is the grouper
They're the same tool doing the same job
The first tool is the grouper; the second is the encoder

feedback.correct: Right. An encoder is fundamentally a code-lookup and validation tool — it knows the coding conventions (what's a valid code, what combinations conflict, what a code's official description is) and helps assign or verify individual codes. A grouper is a downstream tool that takes a finished code set plus a handful of other data points and calculates a payment category (the DRG) and its associated weight. The encoder helps you get the codes right; the grouper tells you what those codes are worth once they're right.
feedback.same: They're genuinely distinct tools with distinct jobs, even though they're often used in the same workflow and sometimes bundled into the same software product — treating them as identical is exactly the loose habit that costs new reviewers time.
feedback.swapped: This has the two roles backwards — code validation and lookup is the encoder's job; DRG and payment-weight calculation is the grouper's job, which happens after the codes are already finalized.

contentSections.concept: **The encoder validates and helps assign individual codes. The grouper takes a finished, validated code set and calculates a payment category from it.** They run in sequence, not in parallel — a grouper's output is only as good as the code set it was fed, which is exactly why a wrong grouper result is very often actually a wrong-code problem one step upstream, not a grouper malfunction.

contentSections.body: This distinction matters for a specific, practical reason: when a DRG assignment looks wrong, the diagnostic question isn't "is the grouper broken" — groupers are stable, well-tested, rules-based software, and they're very rarely the actual source of an error. The question is "what did the grouper receive as input," because a grouper faithfully applying its rules to a slightly wrong code set, or a wrong discharge disposition, produces a wrong DRG with total internal consistency. Chasing a DRG problem at the grouper level, instead of checking the code set and discharge status that fed it, is a fast way to spend an hour finding nothing.

The AI pipeline earlier in this track proposes codes; the encoder validates and helps refine them; the grouper turns the finished set into a payment category. Three tools, three jobs, in that order — and a reviewer's judgment applies differently at each stage: catching a pipeline error is about clinical reading, catching an encoder-flagged conflict is about coding convention knowledge, and catching a grouper-level problem is almost always really about checking the inputs one step back.

contentSections.code:
Ticket: "The grouper assigned the wrong DRG for this stay —
escalating to IT to check if the grouper software has a bug."

(The stay's discharge disposition was entered as
"discharged to home" when the note says the patient
was transferred to a skilled nursing facility.)
contentSections.question: What's the actual problem here?

options.label: A wrong input (discharge disposition) was fed to the grouper — the grouper itself is working correctly
The grouper genuinely has a bug and IT escalation is the right call
The DRG weight tables are out of date

feedback.input: Correct. Discharge disposition is one of the specific inputs a grouper uses, alongside the code set — a transfer to a skilled nursing facility versus a routine home discharge can change the DRG assignment entirely, by design, because post-acute care needs affect resource use. The grouper applied its rules correctly to a wrong input; the fix is correcting the discharge disposition field, not debugging software that isn't broken.
feedback.bug: Escalating to IT sends the problem to the wrong place and delays the actual fix — the grouper's rules-based logic is doing exactly what it's supposed to do with the input it was given.
feedback.tables: There's no evidence pointing at outdated weight tables here — the described discrepancy (a discharge-status data entry error) explains the wrong DRG completely on its own.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A grouper problem almost always turns out to be an input problem one step upstream — checking the code set and the handful of other fields (discharge disposition, principal diagnosis flag, complication/comorbidity indicators) before escalating anything is the fast, usually-correct first move, and it's a skill specific to knowing what a grouper actually consumes.

contentSections.body: When a DRG looks wrong, check the inputs — the code set and discharge status — before suspecting the grouper itself. The grouper is rules-based and rarely the actual problem.

contentSections.title: What a reviewer is actually responsible for verifying

contentSections.body: Not every input to the encoder-grouper chain is a reviewer's job to double-check on every claim — knowing which ones are is what keeps this from turning into re-verifying the entire chart from scratch every time.

contentSections.scenario: Inputs and outputs in the encoder/grouper chain.
contentSections.question: Which of these is realistically part of a coding reviewer's own verification responsibility, rather than something to trust the tool for?

items.label: Whether the codes fed into the grouper actually match the documentation
Whether the discharge disposition field matches what the note says happened
Whether the grouper's internal DRG-weight calculation arithmetic is correct
Whether the encoder's built-in code-conflict rules are up to date with the current year's coding guidelines

explanation.code_accuracy: This is the core of the job this entire track has been building — verifying codes against documentation is squarely a reviewer's responsibility, tool or no tool.
explanation.disposition: Discharge disposition is a data field a reviewer can and should cross-check against the actual discharge note, since it's exactly the kind of input error that produces a plausible-looking but wrong grouper output.
explanation.grouper_math: The internal arithmetic of a well-established, vendor-maintained grouper is not something an individual reviewer is expected to audit — that's the vendor's responsibility, verified through their own testing and certification process.
explanation.encoder_rules: Whether an encoder's rule set reflects the current year's official coding guideline updates is a maintenance responsibility that belongs to whoever administers the software license, not something an individual reviewer checks claim by claim.

contentSections.synthesis: A reviewer's verification job sits at the boundary the tools can't see across: does this code set actually match this documentation, and do the handful of structured fields (discharge disposition, present-on-admission flags) match what actually happened. What happens inside the encoder and grouper once those inputs are correct is the vendor's responsibility, not the reviewer's — and treating everything as equally your job to re-verify is a fast way to burn review time on the wrong layer.

contentSections.body: Your verification responsibility is the boundary between documentation and structured input fields — not the internal logic of tools that are tested and maintained by someone else.

title: EHR navigation without a second monitor
description: Real single-monitor navigation patterns for moving between a note, an encoder, and a review queue without losing your place — and why the naive approach of many open tabs makes this worse, not better.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a single-monitor navigation pattern that avoids losing context between tools
Explain why more open windows or tabs doesn't solve the underlying navigation problem

contentSections.title: Why more windows isn't the fix

contentSections.body: A second monitor costs money not everyone's employer provides, and it costs desk space not everyone's setup has room for — working from a laptop propped on a pillow, one screen is often the real constraint, not a preference. The instinct to compensate with a dozen open browser tabs solves the wrong problem.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer working single-monitor keeps the note, the encoder, and the review queue open in eleven browser tabs, switching between them with Ctrl+Tab as she works a claim.
contentSections.question: What's the actual cost of this approach, beyond just "a lot of tabs"?

options.label: Eleven tabs use too much memory and slow the browser down
Finding the right tab among eleven similar-looking ones costs a small but real re-orientation moment every single switch
There's no real cost — this is a perfectly efficient system

feedback.memory: Modern hardware handles eleven browser tabs without meaningful slowdown in almost all cases — this isn't really the bottleneck worth worrying about.
feedback.reorient: Right. The real cost isn't computational, it's cognitive: scanning eleven similar-looking tab titles to find the right one, every single switch, adds up to a genuinely large amount of small re-orientation friction across a full day — friction that's invisible in the moment but shows up as fatigue and, per the module before this one, eventually as errors.
feedback.fine: The system technically works, but 'works' and 'doesn't cost anything' are different claims — this lesson exists because the hidden cost of constant tab-hunting is real even when nothing ever visibly breaks.

contentSections.mechanism: **Why more tabs doesn't solve single-monitor navigation:** the actual bottleneck isn't screen space, it's finding the thing you need quickly and returning to where you were. A dozen tabs multiplies the search space you have to scan on every switch, which is the opposite of what's needed. The fix is a small, fixed set of pinned, purpose-specific windows or tabs, arranged the same way every time, so switching becomes muscle memory instead of a fresh search.

contentSections.body: A workable single-monitor pattern: two or three fixed tabs, always in the same order, always pinned so they don't get lost among transient ones — the note/EHR, the encoder, and the review queue. A keyboard shortcut (browser-native tab-number shortcuts, or an OS-level window-switcher bound to specific apps) moves between exactly those three without any visual search at all. Anything else — a reference lookup, a coding manual — opens in a fourth, disposable tab that gets closed the moment it's used, so it never joins the fixed set and never has to be hunted for later.
A small, fixed, always-in-the-same-order set of windows beats a large flexible one — the goal is switching without searching, not having everything simultaneously visible.

contentSections.title: Keeping your place across an interruption

contentSections.body: The harder version of this problem isn't switching between three tabs mid-flow — it's coming back to any of them after a real interruption (a phone call, a symptom flare that needs five minutes, the end of a session entirely) and knowing exactly where you were.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in order for resuming a claim after an unplanned interruption.
steps: Check the scratch note for the claim ID and status phrase left before stepping away
Reopen the fixed three-tab set in its usual order
Navigate directly to the noted claim rather than starting from the top of the queue
Re-verify the specific thing the status phrase says was still pending before continuing
contentSections.explanation: The scratch note has to be checked first because everything after depends on knowing where you actually were, not where memory suggests you were. Reopening the fixed tab set in its usual order re-establishes the muscle-memory navigation from the first pod. Going directly to the noted claim, rather than the top of the queue, avoids re-doing work that was already finished. And re-verifying the specific pending item — rather than assuming your own note was complete — catches the case where the interruption happened mid-thought and the note itself is incomplete.

contentSections.body: The single most useful habit here is deliberately cheap: before stepping away, note the claim ID and a one-phrase status ("claim 4471, checked primary dx, still need secondary review") somewhere outside the tools themselves — a sticky note app, a single persistent scratch document, whatever's lowest-friction. This connects directly to the personal working record from the previous module: it's the same instinct (don't trust memory across a gap) applied to a mid-task interruption instead of a mid-day one.
A one-line external note before stepping away — claim ID plus status phrase — is cheap enough to actually do and specific enough to actually rely on.

title: Keyboard-only and low-strain working patterns
description: Reducing mouse dependence and physical strain across a full day of review work — real shortcuts, real ergonomic choices, and the honest limits of what a keyboard-only pattern can cover in tools that weren't built for it.

learningObjectives.text: Apply keyboard-first navigation patterns across the encoder, EHR, and review queue
Identify where a tool's keyboard support is genuinely incomplete and plan around it

contentSections.title: What keyboard-first actually buys you

contentSections.body: A repetitive mouse-reach-and-click, forty times an item, three hundred items a week, adds up to real physical cost for hands and shoulders that are already managing a chronic condition — and most of that reaching is avoidable, because most review software has keyboard paths nobody bothered to learn.

The high-value keyboard patterns worth actually learning, in rough order of payoff: **tab order** through a claim's fields (most encoders and EHRs support logical tab-through, even when it isn't advertised); **find-in-page** (Ctrl/Cmd+F) instead of scrolling and scanning a long note visually; **browser and OS-level tab/window switching shortcuts** instead of mouse-clicking between the fixed set from the previous lesson; and **text expansion** for the handful of phrases typed repeatedly (a query template, a standard escalation note) so a full sentence comes from four keystrokes instead of retyping it.

contentSections.intro: Build a keyboard-first workflow for reviewing one claim, choosing the right tool for each step.

fields.prompt: Scanning a four-page note for a specific term (e.g., "diabetes")
options: Zoom out to see more at once
fields.feedback: Find-in-page jumps directly to every occurrence, which is both faster and less physically demanding than scrolling and visually scanning a long document.

fields.prompt: Moving between a claim's structured fields (diagnosis, procedure, disposition)
options: Tab key, in the form's logical order
Click each field individually with the mouse
Use the browser's address bar to jump between page sections
fields.correctValue: Tab key, in the form's logical order
fields.feedback: Most structured forms support tab order even when it's not obvious from the interface — worth testing once on an unfamiliar tool, since it usually works and eliminates most of the field-to-field mouse reaching.

fields.prompt: Switching between the note, the encoder, and the queue (the fixed set from the previous lesson)
options: A bound keyboard shortcut for each fixed tab position
Alt+Tab through every open window generically
Close and reopen each tool as needed
fields.correctValue: A bound keyboard shortcut for each fixed tab position
fields.feedback: A shortcut bound to a specific position (browser tab-number shortcuts, or an OS window-switcher bound to named apps) goes directly to the right tool without the generic Alt+Tab cycling through everything else open.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these three choices are exotic — find-in-page, tab order, and bound shortcuts are all standard features most people simply never learned to reach for by default. The payoff compounds specifically because it's the same four or five patterns applied dozens of times a day, not because any one of them is individually dramatic.

contentSections.body: Find-in-page, tab order, and bound switching shortcuts cover most of a day's routine mouse use — the payoff comes from repetition, not from any one trick.

contentSections.title: Where keyboard-only genuinely runs out

contentSections.body: Being honest about the limits here matters as much as the techniques themselves — a tool that claims full keyboard accessibility and doesn't quite deliver it is worse to plan around than one that's upfront about a mouse-dependent step.

contentSections.scenario: Common review-software interactions.
contentSections.question: Which of these routinely resist a clean keyboard-only path, even in well-built tools?

items.label: A searchable dropdown for selecting a specific diagnosis code from thousands of options
Drag-and-drop reordering of a code list's priority
Freeform annotation or highlighting on a scanned (image-based, not text) document
Typing a free-text query note into a comment box

explanation.dropdown_search: A searchable dropdown, despite looking complex, is usually one of the better-supported keyboard patterns — type to filter, arrow keys to move, Enter to select is a very common, well-implemented pattern.
explanation.drag_reorder: Drag-and-drop genuinely has no reliable universal keyboard equivalent unless the software specifically built one (some do, with 'move up/move down' buttons as an alternative — worth checking for, since it's not guaranteed) — this is a real, honest gap in many tools.
explanation.canvas_annotation: Marking up a scanned image (rather than selectable text) is one of the genuine remaining gaps — there's no text to tab through or find-in-page, and freeform marking generally needs pointer input of some kind, whether mouse, touch, or stylus.
explanation.text_field: A standard text box is fully keyboard-native by default — typing directly into it needs no special technique at all.

contentSections.synthesis: The honest gaps cluster around genuinely spatial interactions — drag-and-drop, freeform marking on an image — where there's no text or discrete list for a keyboard to move through. Knowing these specific two or three gap categories in advance means planning around them deliberately (a touchpad's tap-to-click at minimum, a stylus, or asking whether the tool has a button-based alternative) instead of discovering the gap mid-task on a bad-hands day.

contentSections.body: Drag-and-drop and freeform image annotation are the honest remaining gaps in most keyboard-first workflows — plan a fallback for those specifically, rather than assuming everything will have a keyboard path.

title: Reference lookups that don't cost you three minutes
description: Building a fast, personal reference system for the handful of lookups (coding guideline sections, payer-specific rules, combination-code tables) that recur constantly — instead of a fresh search engine query every time.

learningObjectives.text: Build a personal quick-reference system for recurring lookup needs
Distinguish a lookup worth caching personally from one that needs a fresh check every time

contentSections.title: The three-minute tax on a lookup you've done before

contentSections.body: This is the fourth time this month you've needed to check whether a particular combination code applies, and it's the fourth time you've searched the coding manual from scratch, scrolled to the right section, and re-read the same three paragraphs — three minutes each time, twelve minutes this month, on something you already figured out three times already.

contentSections.scenario: A coder tracks how often, across a month, she looks something up that she's already looked up before — the same guideline section, the same payer rule, the same combination-code table.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of her total lookup time, across the month, goes to re-finding something she'd already found before?
contentSections.explanation: For most reviewers, the majority of lookup time — often more than half — goes to re-finding a small set of things looked up repeatedly, not genuinely new questions. This is exactly the kind of cost that's invisible day to day (three minutes doesn't feel like much) and adds up to a real, recoverable chunk of time once actually measured, which is why building a personal reference for the repeat lookups specifically is worth the modest upfront effort.

contentSections.body: The fix isn't memorizing more — it's a small, personal, searchable reference document (a single page, a set of tagged notes, whatever tool is lowest-friction) that holds exactly the handful of things that keep recurring: the combination-code pattern from an earlier module's error-cluster work, the specific payer's documentation quirks, the guideline section number for a rule checked constantly. The first time something is looked up, it goes in the manual the normal way. The second time the same thing comes up, it goes into the personal reference instead — the manual lookup was the cost of building the reference, not a cost to pay every time after.
Most repeat lookup time goes to a small, recurring set of the same few questions — a personal reference built after the second occurrence of each one recovers most of that time.

contentSections.title: What belongs in a personal reference, and what doesn't

contentSections.body: Not everything worth looking up once is worth caching — a personal reference that tries to hold everything becomes exactly as slow to search as the original manual, just smaller and less authoritative.

contentSections.scenario: A coder is deciding whether to add a lookup to her personal reference: a payer-specific rule about documentation requirements for a particular procedure, checked three times this month; versus a one-off question about a rare congenital condition's code, looked up once for a chart that's unlikely to recur.
contentSections.question: Which one belongs in the personal reference?

options.label: The payer rule, checked three times
The rare congenital condition code
Both, to be thorough

feedback.payer: Right. A recurring lookup — something checked multiple times already, for a payer or claim type that comes up regularly — is exactly what a personal reference is for. It's already demonstrated it'll be needed again.
feedback.rare: A genuinely rare, unlikely-to-recur lookup doesn't earn a place in the personal reference — caching it costs upkeep (keeping it findable, keeping it current if rules change) for something that may never come up again, which is a bad trade.
feedback.both: Adding everything defeats the reference's purpose — its value comes specifically from being small enough to scan quickly, which requires being selective about what gets included, not comprehensive.

contentSections.concept: **The test for the personal reference: has this specific thing already recurred, and is it likely to recur again given the claim mix this reviewer actually works?** A rule checked once for an unusual case doesn't pass that test even if it took a while to find; a rule checked three times for routine claim types does, even if any single lookup was quick. Frequency of recurrence, not difficulty of the original lookup, is the right filter.

contentSections.body: Worth revisiting the reference periodically too — a payer changes a rule, a coding guideline gets updated annually, and a stale personal reference that nobody prunes eventually costs more (a wrong answer trusted with the same speed as a right one) than it saves. A quarterly five-minute skim to flag anything that might be outdated is enough to keep it trustworthy without turning maintenance into its own chore.
Cache what's demonstrated it recurs, not what was merely hard to find once — and prune it periodically, since a fast wrong answer is worse than a slow right one.

title: Setting up a workstation you can use lying down
description: Building a genuinely usable review setup for lying-down or reclined work — the real hardware and software choices that make this possible, and the honest limits of what's achievable that way.

learningObjectives.text: Specify a workstation configuration that supports reclined or lying-down review work
Identify which parts of the review workflow remain genuinely hard in a reclined position

contentSections.title: What actually makes a setup work lying down

contentSections.body: A laptop balanced on a stomach, screen tilted at an unreadable angle, wrists bent at a strain-inducing angle to type — that's not a lying-down setup, that's an upright setup attempted while lying down, and it fails within twenty minutes for reasons that have nothing to do with willpower.

contentSections.scenario: Hardware and setup choices for reclined review work.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuinely load-bearing for making reclined work actually usable, not just theoretically possible?

items.label: An adjustable laptop or tablet stand/mount that holds the screen at eye level without hand support
A separate, lightweight wireless keyboard usable at a relaxed wrist angle rather than the laptop's built-in one
The specific brand of laptop
Voice-to-text for longer free-text entries (query notes, escalation writeups) as an alternative to sustained typing

explanation.stand: This is the single highest-payoff piece of hardware — without it, the screen angle problem alone makes extended reclined work physically unsustainable, regardless of anything else in the setup.
explanation.keyboard: A laptop's built-in keyboard forces a specific hand position relative to the screen; a separate keyboard can be positioned independently, at whatever angle and distance is actually comfortable while reclined.
explanation.brightness: Brand isn't the relevant variable — what matters is the specific features (adjustable brightness, matte vs. glossy screen for glare, size) not which company made it, and most brands offer comparable options at this level.
explanation.voice: For the longer free-text writing this track has covered (escalation reports, query notes, the reviewer's own working-record entries), voice-to-text removes sustained typing entirely for exactly the tasks where hand strain accumulates fastest.

contentSections.synthesis: Three things do most of the real work: a stand that gets the screen to eye level without hands holding it, a keyboard that can be positioned independently of the screen, and voice input for the longest free-text stretches. None of this is exotic or expensive by comparison to a full second-monitor setup — it's specifically chosen for what reclined work actually needs, which is different from what an upright desk setup needs.

contentSections.body: A stand, an independently-positioned keyboard, and voice input for longer text cover most of what makes reclined work genuinely sustainable — not brand, not price, specifically those three things.

contentSections.title: What's still genuinely hard, and planning around it honestly

contentSections.body: This lesson doesn't end with "and now everything works lying down" — some parts of the job stay genuinely harder reclined, and pretending otherwise sets up a bad day when one of them shows up.

contentSections.question: A coder has a genuinely hard drag-and-drop task to do and it's a bad-hands day where reclined is the only realistic position. What's the honest, sustainable move — force through the drag-and-drop reclined, or something else?
contentSections.answer: Check first whether the tool has a button-based alternative to the drag-and-drop (many do, even if not obviously advertised); if not, this specific task may be one worth batching for a better-capacity moment rather than forcing through reclined, since forcing a genuinely hard interaction through a worse ergonomic setup on an already-hard day compounds two costs at once instead of addressing either.
contentSections.hint: This connects to the queue-craft module's stopping-rule logic — not every task has to happen right now, in this position, on this day.

contentSections.body: The honest remaining friction points, carried over directly from the two earlier lessons in this module: drag-and-drop interactions and freeform annotation on scanned images are already hard with a mouse on a desk, and they get harder with a touchpad at an awkward reclined angle.
